api_metadata.summary:
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA; 42 U.S.C. §§4321 et. seq.) sets forth a national policy with respect to environmental quality and a procedural framework for integrating environmental considerations into federal decisionmaking (i.e., through environmental review). The range of federal agencies and actions subject to NEPA is broad and includes activities such as resource management decisions, issuing permits, and funding infrastructure projects. Under NEPA, federal agencies must evaluate reasonably foreseeable adverse environmental effects, consider a reasonable range of alternatives, and prepare required documentation (i.e., environmental documents) for “major [f]ederal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.” Federal agencies may also engage other governmental entities, project applicants (i.e., project sponsors), and members of the public to identify issues, obtain relevant information, and inform environmental analyses. 
Federally recognized Tribes (Tribes) may participate in environmental reviews for various reasons. In some circumstances, federal action may arise because a Tribe proposes an activity that requires federal agency approval or involves an associated federal authorization. In other circumstances, federal action may occur on or affect tribal lands, treaty-protected rights, or resources in which the United States has responsibilities under applicable federal law. This In Focus provides an overview of the various ways in which Tribes may engage in the environmental review process under NEPA.
Tribal Roles and Participation in NEPA Reviews
A Tribe’s role in an environmental review varies depending on whether it proposes an activity requiring federal action or participates in the review of an action proposed by another entity. Potential tribal roles are outlined in this section.
Project Sponsor
A Tribe may serve as a project sponsor when it proposes an activity that requires a federal agency decision. In these circumstances, the Tribe may provide project information and other materials needed for the environmental review, while the federal agency remains responsible for the contents of the environmental document and making the federal decision. For some actions (e.g., leases or rights-of-way) on tribal lands, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) is primarily responsible for authorization. 
Joint Lead Agency
NEPA assigns responsibilities for environmental review to the federal agency proposing a federal action or responsible for authorizing certain actions. The federal agency conducting the environmental review is typically the lead agency, but Tribes may participate in other formal roles. For many federal actions involving Tribes, the BIA is the lead agency, and in some circumstances, Tribes may participate as joint lead agencies. As a joint lead agency, a Tribe would share responsibilities related to a proposed action, including supervising the environmental review process, coordinating with other agencies, and overseeing and developing a schedule for completing the environmental review and any associated federal permits or related authorizations. Although joint lead agency arrangements involving Tribes are less common than cooperating agency participation—discussed in the next section—they may be used for proposed actions involving BIA authorizations, proposed actions affecting tribal lands, and other shared federal and tribal decisionmaking responsibilities.
Cooperating Agency
Under NEPA, the lead agency may invite any federal, state, tribal, or local agency with “jurisdiction by law or special expertise” relevant to any environmental impact to participate as a cooperating agency. A Tribe may also request cooperating agency status where appropriate. Cooperating agencies may, among other things, assist in identifying issues for analysis, developing alternatives, providing technical information, and preparing environmental documents. Acting as a cooperating agency may require a commitment of resources and time to meet the lead agency’s schedule. Although the lead agency remains responsible for the analysis, the environmental review, and any resulting decisions, cooperating agency status may provide Tribes with opportunities to engage earlier and more directly in the development of a proposed action and the environmental analysis than would otherwise occur through public participation.
Public Participation in the Environmental Review Process
Tribes may also provide input on environmental reviews through public participation opportunities. Until recently, NEPA implementation was guided by government-wide regulations, promulgated by the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ). These regulations required federal agencies to request comments from the public, as well as any state, local, or tribal government that may be affected by the proposed action during the preparation of certain environmental documents. Effective April 2025, CEQ rescinded those regulations and directed federal agencies to replace these regulations with federal-agency-specific procedures that may or may not include similar requests for public comment opportunities. Depending on agency procedures (e.g., DOI Handbook of NEPA Procedures) and level of review, these opportunities may include participation during scoping, review of draft environmental documents, submission of written comments, or public meeting input.
Federal Delegation of Authorizations and Environmental Reviews to Tribes
At times, Congress has enacted statutes that allow Tribes to authorize certain activities on tribal lands without case-by-case approval by the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary, as delegated to the BIA), provided the Tribe has an environmental review process meeting specified statutory requirements. For example, the Helping Expedite and Advance Responsible Tribal Homeownership Act of 2012 (HEARTH Act, 25 U.S.C. §415(h)) authorizes Tribes to approve tribal leases on tribal lands executed under tribal regulations approved by the Secretary. In addition, the Indian Tribal Energy Development and Self Determination Act of 2005 (25 U.S.C. §3504(e)) allows qualifying Tribes to propose tribal energy resource agreements (TERAs) with the Secretary. If the Secretary approves a TERA, that Tribe can enter into leases, business agreements, or rights-of-way to develop energy resources on tribal lands without secretarial approval. Under both statutes, Tribes must conduct environmental reviews that meet specified criteria. 
Other Opportunities for Tribal Participation 
In addition to participating in these NEPA roles, Tribes may engage with federal agencies pursuant to other statutory authorities. These other authorities differ in their legal basis, purpose, and procedural requirements, but federal agencies often coordinate compliance within the NEPA process to reduce duplication and facilitate informed decisionmaking. For example, federal agencies integrate their environmental reviews with reviews under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. Information gathered during one engagement (e.g., information regarding cultural or environmental resources) may also inform the NEPA analyses. Thus, tribal participation during an environmental review often reflects compliance with several overlapping authorities rather than NEPA alone. 
Beyond engaging with federal agencies pursuant to these statutory authorities, Tribes may request government-to-government consultations pursuant to the federal trust responsibility, treaty obligations, executive orders, or agency consultation policies. The federal trust responsibility is a legal obligation under which the United States—through treaties, acts of Congress, and court decisions—“has charged itself with moral obligations of the highest responsibility and trust” toward Tribes and tribal members. Government-to-government consultation may include correspondence, meetings, site visits, workshops, or other discussions regarding the proposed action. Tribal engagement through government-to-government consultation is different than public review of environmental documents because it typically involves meetings and communication between tribal and federal leaders, whereas during public review, Tribes engage through the same procedural opportunities available to all members of the public and other entities. 
Selected Issues for Congress
Members of Congress have considered legislation addressing tribal engagement in NEPA reviews and implementation.
Consistency of NEPA requirements. Following the rescission of the CEQ NEPA regulations, opportunities for Tribes to participate in environmental reviews and comment on draft environmental documents may vary among federal agencies and project types. While some tribal groups asserted support for the Trump Administration for “reducing unnecessary federal regulations and streamlining overly complex permitting processes that disproportionately burden” Tribes, they also urged Congress to give CEQ regulatory control over NEPA again, and to add tribal consultation requirements to NEPA. 
Application of NEPA to tribal lands and resources. NEPA is silent regarding how an agency should analyze or determine the impact of proposed actions affecting tribal lands and resources. The Standardizing Permitting and Expediting Economic Development Act (H.R. 4776) and Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (S. 5653) would amend NEPA to direct federal agencies to presume that declining to proceed (taking no action) on a tribal proposal would negatively affect the Tribe. The House Committee on Natural Resources (majority) asserted that this directive would promote tribal sovereignty. In addition, some Tribes have advocated for more power to decide whether an environmental review is necessary and how it might be conducted for projects on tribal lands. For example, the Southern Ute Indian Tribe has stated that it increased efficiencies after developing its own environmental review process under the HEARTH Act. Yet this approach may create inconsistencies in environmental review practices among Tribes and between Tribes and federal agencies.
Consideration of tribal input in federal decisions. Congress may choose to constrict, maintain, or expand statutes governing consideration of tribal input in federal decisionmaking. As discussed above, Congress has issued some direction to federal agencies on when and how to consider tribal input. While Tribes have often sought increased influence in NEPA reviews, federal agencies may find it challenging to weigh tribal input against other statutory mandates and priorities. 
Federal and Tribal Capacity. Some federal agencies and Tribes have identified limitations in agency and tribal capacity as hindering meaningful engagement, including for environmental reviews. In a GAO report on government-to-government consultation, many federal agencies cited “constraints on agency staff, financial resources, or both to support consultation.” Tribal participation in environmental reviews may also require the expenditure of tribal resources. At times, Congress has appropriated funding that has been used to help Tribes engage in environmental reviews. For example, P.L. 117-169 appropriated $350 million to the Permitting Council’s Environmental Review Improvement Fund. The Permitting Council set aside $5 million from the fund in 2023, and an additional $10 million in 2024, to support tribal engagement in the environmental review and authorization process for FAST-41-covered infrastructure projects.

api_metadata.summary:
Introduction
The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) was enacted in 1938 with the goal of establishing minimum national labor standards, including for weekly hours of work. To that end, the FLSA requires that employers pay covered, nonexempt employees at a rate of one-and-a-half times their regular rate of pay for hours worked in excess of 40 per week in a given job. This In Focus provides an overview of the FLSA overtime pay requirements and recent legislative proposals to amend them.
General Provisions
Section 7(a)(1) of the FLSA (29 U.S.C. §207(a)(1)) provides the following:
Except as otherwise provided in this section, no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.
The Regular Rate of Pay
An employee’s regular rate of pay is calculated in each workweek in which the employee is entitled to overtime pay. It is an hourly rate determined using the following formula: 
/
The regular rate must include all compensation “for employment paid to, or on behalf of, the employee” in the workweek in which overtime hours occur. Total compensation includes the worker’s hourly rate of pay and other employment-related payments received during the workweek, such as nondiscretionary bonuses (e.g., productivity-based bonuses), on-call pay required by state and local laws, and the reasonable value of meals or lodging provided as compensation to employees. 
Some payments to employees are not considered to be compensation, and the act explicitly excludes them from the regular rate. These statutory exclusions include certain employer gifts, paid leave (e.g., paid sick leave, paid holidays), employer contributions to the employee’s health plan, and payments for reimbursable business expenses, among others. 
Example: Overtime Pay for an Hourly Worker
The regular rate of pay in a workweek in which an employee earned an hourly wage of $12 and worked 46 hours would be
/
The employee would be entitled to $12 per hour for 40 hours of work and $18 per hour (=1.5 x $12 per hour) for the 6 overtime hours, a total of $588 for the workweek.  
Example: Overtime Pay for an Hourly Worker Who Received a Production Bonus
If the worker received a $46 production bonus in addition to her hourly rate of $12, her regular rate of pay would be
/
In this instance, the employee would be entitled to $13 per hour for 40 hours of work and $19.50 per hour (=1.5 x $13) for the 6 overtime hours, for a total of $637 for the workweek.  
Example: Overtime Pay for a Tipped Worker
The FLSA permits employers to count up to $5.12 (per hour) in tips received by a tipped worker toward the employer’s minimum wage obligation. (The federal minimum wage is currently $7.25 per hour.) For example, an employer would meet its FLSA minimum wage obligation if it paid at least $21.30 to a tipped worker in a workweek in which the employee worked 10 hours (i.e., $2.13 per hour for 10 hours) and received tips of at least $51.20 (i.e., $5.12 per hour for 10 hours). Employers may also apply the tip credit—up to $5.12 per hour—toward their FLSA overtime pay obligations. 
Employers must use the employee’s full wage (i.e., at least the federal minimum wage) when calculating the regular rate of pay for a tipped worker and must include service charges, commissions, bonuses, and other compensation received by the tipped employee during the workweek. Any tips received by the employee in excess of the tip credit need not be included in the regular rate because such tips are not compensation paid by the employer to the employee.
For example, the regular rate for a tipped worker whose employer claimed a tip credit of $5.12 per hour, and who worked 50 hours in a workweek and received at least $256 in tips (=50 hours x $5.12 per hour), would be
/
Such an employee would be entitled to $7.25 per hour for 40 hours of work and $10.875 per hour (=1.5 x $7.25 per hour) for the 10 overtime hours, for a total of $398.75 for the workweek. Because the employee earned at least $256 (=$5.12 per hour x 50 hours) in tips during the work week, the employer could claim the maximum tip credit ($256 = $5.12 per hour x 50 hours) and pay a direct cash wage of $142.75 to the employee.
State and Local Government Employees’ Compensatory Time Option
The FLSA allows covered, nonexempt state and local government employees to receive compensatory time off (comp time)—paid time off in lieu of overtime pay—for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. Comp time is calculated at a rate that is at least one-and-a-half times the number of overtime hours worked. 
An employer and employee must agree that the employer will provide comp time in lieu of overtime pay. The agreement may be through a collective bargaining agreement or, if there is no such agreement, between the employer and individual employees. 
In general, state and local government employees may accrue up to 240 hours of comp time. Law enforcement, fire protection, emergency response personnel, and employees engaged in seasonal activities may accrue up to 480 hours of comp time. An employee must be allowed to use comp time on the date requested, unless doing so would “unduly disrupt” the operations of the agency. Employers must compensate employees for unused accrued compensatory time.
Overtime Pay Exemptions
While generally broad in coverage, the FLSA exempts several worker groups from its overtime provisions. For example, agricultural employees, certain domestic service employees, some transportation workers (including certain interstate truck drivers and taxicab drivers), movie theater employees, and some salaried executive, administrative, and professional employees, among others, are not entitled to overtime pay under the FLSA. 
The act also provides for partial exemptions from its overtime pay requirements for some groups of workers. For example, employees engaged in law enforcement and fire protection and employed by public agencies may be paid overtime on the basis of longer work periods (e.g., up to 28 consecutive days) and have higher work-hours thresholds for overtime pay (e.g., for a 14-day work period, such law enforcement personnel must receive overtime pay after 86 hours worked). 
FLSA Does Not Govern Scheduling 
The FLSA does not limit the number of hours an employee may work (e.g., there are no daily or weekly limits), and it does not govern how work hours are scheduled. For example, the act does not limit an employer’s ability to schedule 7 consecutive 24-hour workdays (but would generally require overtime pay for hours worked beyond 40 for covered, nonexempt employees). 
Enforcement
The FLSA authorizes the Department of Labor (DOL) to conduct workplace inspections and investigations to determine if FLSA violations have occurred and to enforce the FLSA provisions. 
Based on the results of an investigation, DOL may order an employer to pay back wages and liquidated damages to affected employees, may assess civil money penalties for repeat or willful violations of the FLSA overtime provisions, or both. If DOL is unable to administratively resolve a dispute, it may file a lawsuit in a U.S. district court on behalf of employees for back wages and liquidated damages, or injunctive relief (e.g., to restrain violations such as unlawful withholding of pay or retaliation against employees who cooperate with DOL). DOL may also seek an order for payment of civil money penalties from a DOL Administrative Law Judge and can recommend criminal prosecution for willful violations.
In lieu of action by DOL, employees may file a lawsuit in U.S. district court for back wages and liquidated damages, or injunctive relief. Lawsuits may be filed individually or as collective actions. A prevailing employee may recoup reasonable attorney fees and court costs from an employer who is found to violate the act.
Recent Legislative Proposals
Some bills introduced in the 119th Congress have proposed various amendments to the FLSA overtime pay provisions and related exemptions. 
Proposed amendments to the overtime pay requirement include the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act (H.R. 10323/S. 5384) and the Double the Wage for Overtime Act of 2026 (H.R. 9216/S. 5268). 
Proposed amendments to the regular rate statutory exclusions include the Empowering Employer Child and Elder Care Solutions Act (H.R. 2270) and the Valuing Employee Stock Today Act (H.R. 8660). 
Proposals to add, modify, or remove FLSA overtime exemptions include the Outdoor Recreational Outfitting and Guiding Act (H.R. 3499), the Ensuring Access to Affordable and Quality Home Care for Seniors and People with Disabilities Act (H.R. 2304), the Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026 (H.R. 8868/S. 4551), the Guaranteeing Overtime for Truckers Act (H.R. 1962/S. 893), and the Fairness for Farmworkers Act (H.R. 10273/S. 5304).
The Working Families Flexibility Act of 2025 (H.R. 2870/S. 1158) would allow private sector employees to receive compensatory time in lieu of overtime pay.
The Protect Local Farms Act (H.R. 240) would preempt certain state laws entitling agricultural employees to overtime pay.

api_metadata.summary:
Introduction
Congress has historically sought to help small, “socially and economically disadvantaged” business owners overcome barriers to participating in federal contracting and compete in the national economy through the Small Business Administration’s (SBA's) 8(a) Business Development Program, (commonly known as the “8(a) program”). Congress has also established annual goals for small business participation in federal contracting, including a goal of awarding 5% of prime and subcontract awards to small, disadvantaged businesses (see CRS Insight IN12018, Federal Small Business Contracting Goals, by R. Corinne Blackford). 
For eligible businesses, 8(a) program participation offers federal contracting preferences such as federal contract set-asides and sole-source contracts. 8(a) program participants also receive dedicated business development support, including mentorship, training, and counseling designed to enhance the competitiveness of participant businesses and their long-term viability. For background on the 8(a) program, see CRS Report R44844, SBA’s 8(a) Business Development Program: Legislative and Program History, by R. Corinne Blackford. 
Although the 8(a) program was authorized in 1978 for the benefit of small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals, Congress expanded the program in the 1980s to include entity-owned small businesses, owned by disadvantaged groups. The eligible groups or entities include
Community Development Corporations (CDCs)
Alaska Native Corporations (ANCs)
Indian tribes
Native Hawaiian Organizations (NHOs)
This In Focus highlights group- or entity-owned firm participation in the 8(a) program because these firms participate under somewhat different terms than small businesses owned by individuals.  
Legislation Expanding 8(a) Program Eligibility to Groups/Entities
CDC Eligibility 
CDCs were the first type of entity made eligible for the 8(a) program. Congress created CDCs through the Community Economic Development Act of 1981 and instructed the SBA to issue regulations ensuring that CDCs could participate in the 8(a) program (P.L. 97-35, Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981). Codified at 42 U.S.C. §9802, a CDC is defined as
a nonprofit organization responsible to residents of the area it serves which is receiving financial assistance under part A of this subchapter [42 U.S.C. §§9805 et seq.] and any organization more than 50 percent of which is owned by such an organization, or otherwise controlled by such an organization, or designated by such an organization for the purpose of this subchapter [42 U.S.C. §§9801 et seq.].
Tribal and ANC Eligibility
In 1986, two additional owner-groups, Indian tribes and ANCs, became eligible for the 8(a) program when Congress passed legislation providing that they were socially disadvantaged for 8(a) program purposes (P.L. 99-272, Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985; 15 U.S.C. §637(a)(13) and 15 U.S.C. §637(a)(4)). An ANC is
any Regional Corporation, Village Corporation, Urban Corporation, or Group Corporation organized under the laws of the State of Alaska in accordance with the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, as amended (43 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.).
For program purposes, an Indian tribe is defined at 13 C.F.R. §124.3 as
any Indian tribe, band, nation, or other organized group or community of Indians, including any ANC, which is recognized as eligible for the special programs and services provided by the United States to Indians because of their status as Indians, or is recognized as such by the State in which the tribe, band, nation, group, or community resides. 
Congress passed legislation that deemed ANCs “economically disadvantaged” in 1992 (P.L. 102-415, Alaska Land Status Technical Corrections Act of 1992). In contrast, a tribe must prove economic disadvantage the first time a tribally owned firm applies to the 8(a) Program (13 C.F.R. §124.109(b)(2)).
NHO Eligibility
Congress made NHOs eligible for the program by legislation enacted in 1988 (P.L. 100-656, Business Opportunity Development Reform Act of 1988). An NHO is defined as
any community service organization serving Native Hawaiians in the State of Hawaii which (A) is a nonprofit corporation that has filed articles of incorporation with the director (or the designee thereof) of the Hawaii Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, or any successor agency, (B) is controlled by Native Hawaiians, and (C) whose business activities will principally benefit such Native Hawaiians.
Like tribes, NHOs must prove economic disadvantage the first time an NHO-owned firm applies to the 8(a) program (13 C.F.R. §124.110(c)). 
Terms of Participation
Certain terms of participation apply to all 8(a) participants, including those owned by eligible groups. These include that the firm be “small” according to SBA size standards, be a for-profit business, be “unconditionally owned and controlled” by the disadvantaged individual or entity, demonstrate potential for success, and be of good character (applies to officers, directors, and shareholders owning more than a 20% interest in the business, or to all a firm’s “principals” in the case of CDCs). At the same time, firms owned by CDCs, tribes, ANCs, and NHOs may receive benefits not available to individually-owned firms. 
Sole-Source Contract Value
Group-owned firms may receive sole-source contracts beyond the sole-source award limits imposed on individually-owned 8(a) program participants. An 8(a) firm owned by an individual may receive a sole-source contract as long as it does not exceed $5.5 million (or $8.5 million for manufacturing contracts) (48 C.F.R. §19.805-1(b)(1)-(2)). Furthermore, an individually-owned firm may not receive additional sole-source awards once it has received a combined total of $168,500,000 in competitive contracts (via 8(a) set-asides) and sole-source contracts during its participation in the 8(a) program (13 C.F.R. §124.519). 
Per  P.L. 109-148, §8020, NHO-owned firms may only receive contracts valued over the 8(a) sole-source limits from the Department of Defense (DOD), which is using a secondary Department of War designation” under Executive Order 14347 dated September 5, 2025. 
While the 8(a) sole-source contract limits do not generally apply to group-owned firms (as mentioned, they do apply to NHO-owned firms that receive nondefense contracts), written justifications of large sole-source awards are sometimes required. A written justification for a sole-source award to a tribally- or ANC-owned firm is required for contracts in excess of $30 million, or in excess of $100 million in the case of defense contracts (P.L. 111-84;  P.L. 116-92); a written justification for a sole-source DOD award to an NHO-owned firm is also required for contracts in excess of $100 million. 
Program Participation Duration
Individuals may participate in the program for a single nine-year period (13 C.F.R. §124.108(b); 13 C.F.R. §124.2) while groups may may confer their eligibility status upon different firms on multiple occasions. This allows groups to indefinitely participate in the 8(a) program by owning multiple firms, with limitations; groups may also own more than one 8(a) program participant at a time, with limitations. Groups may not own 51% or more of another firm that “either at the time of [8(a) program] application or within the previous two years,” obtains the majority of its revenue from the same “primary” industry as another one of its firms (13 C.F.R. §124.109(c)(3)(ii); 13 C.F.R. §124.110(f); and 13 C.F.R. §124.111(d)). Groups may own multiple firms that “conduct secondary business” in the same industry, and that earn less than 50% of their revenue in the same primary industry. 
Socially Disadvantaged Status
The SBA has recently proposed to revise the criteria by which individuals establish their social disadvantage in 8(a) program applications. The proposal would not affect firms owned by CDCs, tribes, ANCs, or NHOs. For more information, see CRS Insight IN12698, Proposed SBA Rule Would Establish New Test for Social Disadvantage Under 8(a) Program, by April J. Anderson and R. Corinne Blackford.  
Community Benefits Reporting Requirements
Group-owned firms must report the community benefits of program participation for tribes, ANCs, NHOs, and CDCs. SBA regulations (13 C.F.R. §124.604) state
As part of its annual financial statement submission (see § 124.602), each Participant owned by a Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC must submit to SBA information showing how the Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC has provided benefits to the Tribal or native members and/or the Tribal, native or other community due to the Tribe’s/ANC's/NHO's/CDC’s participation in the 8(a) BD program through one or more firms. This data includes information relating to funding cultural programs, employment assistance, jobs, scholarships, internships, subsistence activities, and other services provided by the Tribe, ANC, NHO or CDC to the affected community.
Federal Contracts Awarded
According to data published in the SBA Procurement Scorecard for FY2025, group-owned firms make up about 16% of firms in the program and received 67% of the contract award dollars made to 8(a) firms in FY2025. GSA’s Small Business Goaling Reports show that 8(a) contract dollars (to any type of participant) have risen in the past five fiscal years. As shown in the table below, 8(a) procedure contract dollars ranged from about $20 billion to $25 billion each fiscal year through FY2025.

This figure has been estimated using SBA Procurement Scorecard data for small disadvantaged businesses in combination with government-wide Goaling Report data due to a Department of State data error. 
Congressional Issues
In recent years, the 8(a) program has faced a constitutional challenge to the definition of social disadvantage previously used in the program. In addition, SBA administrative actions renewed debate on the meaning of “social disadvantage” and legislation (H.R. 8511 and S. 4390) eliminating statutory references to disadvantaged individuals and businesses have been introduced.

Introduction
A federal student loan made under Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (P.L. 89-329), as amended, is considered delinquent the first day after a borrower fails to make a scheduled payment. The Department of Education (ED), through its contracted loan servicers, reports delinquencies to the nationwide, private consumer reporting agencies (CRAs; i.e., Equifax, Experian, TransUnion, Innovis) after 90 days or more of delinquency. Generally, a loan is in default after 270 days of a missed scheduled payment, which is reported to CRAs. 
Since 2020, the portfolio of ED-held federal student loans (ED-held loans) has experienced unusual fluctuations in delinquency and default trends. This In Focus highlights these trends and how various loan-servicing-related issues may have affected these patterns and borrower credit scores. For purposes of this In Focus, loan servicing refers to daily management of a loan. The tasks associated with loan servicing are typically performed by ED-contracted servicers. Their duties include issuing billing statements, collecting regular payments, administering forbearances and alternative repayment plans for past-due borrowers, and reporting loan status to CRAs.
Delinquency and Default Trends
Borrowers of ED-held loans were afforded up to two periods of loan repayment relief in response to and following the COVID-19 pandemic. First, a series of congressional- and Administration-authorized forbearances suspended borrowers’ monthly payment obligations between March 2020 and August 2023 (the payment pause). Second, after P.L. 118-5 ended the payment pause, ED instituted an on-ramp policy, from September 2023 through September 2024. Under this policy, monthly student loan payments were due, but ED placed borrowers more than 90 days delinquent in a retroactive administrative forbearance. This placed a loan’s status to “current repayment” (i.e., not delinquent) and delayed certain consequences of loan delinquency, such as negative credit reporting, until January 2025. 
In light of these policies, notable shifts in delinquency rate patterns of ED-held loans began in March 2020. Similar shifts in default rates occurred several months later at a more gradual pace, as both policies effectively prevented loans from entering delinquency or default. (Loans in default prior to the policies’ implementation remained in default during the policies’ effective dates unless a borrower took steps to resolve the default). In the pre-pandemic period from FY2017 Q1 to FY2020 Q1, between 6% and 8% of loans were 31-270 days delinquent. This rate declined to 0% in FY2020 Q3, the first full quarter in which the payment pause was in effect. The delinquency rate remained at 0% through FY2023 Q4, reflecting the impact of the pandemic-era forbearance policies.
Figure 1 shows that the share of borrowers with better credit scores (teal & purple) generally grew relative to those with weaker credit scores (red & blue) a bit more beginning in 2020. However, these data may not fully reflect a borrower’s actual creditworthiness, as they overlap with the COVID-19 student loan forbearance and on-ramp policies.
Figure 1. Student Loan Borrowers by Credit Score
2004-2024
/
Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 2025 Student Loan Update (direct download). 
Note: Includes borrowers of non-ED-held student loans.
Additionally, the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston found that for borrowers with ED-held loans affected by the payment pause, their credit scores increased to a greater extent than did scores of individuals without student loans. Their analysis suggests that a loan servicing practice—forbearance—rather than a borrower’s ability to repay their debt influenced the rise in credit scores.
Following the static student loan delinquency and default rates of the pandemic era, loan portfolio volatility rose along with the adoption of new federal policies. Figure 2 shows rising delinquencies that are transitioning into defaults over the FY2023 Q4 to FY2026 Q3 period. The rate of recipients with ED-held loans who were 31-270 days delinquent increased from 0% in FY2023 Q4 to 16% the following quarter. Borrowers who exited retroactive administrative forbearance in FY2025 Q1 without curing their delinquency or newly became 31-90 days delinquent transitioned to being 91-270 days delinquent in FY2025 Q2. The default rate remained relatively steady until increasing from 12% (5.3 million recipients) in FY2025 Q3 to 19% (8.8 million recipients) by the next quarter. Over the same period, the share of recipients with loans that were 91-270 days delinquent decreased from 12% (5.5 million) to 4% (1.9 million), likely representing a substantial portion of delinquent borrowers transitioning into default status.
Figure 2. ED-Held Loans: Delinquency, Default Rates 
FY2023 Q4 to FY2026 Q3
/
Source: CRS analysis; U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid Data Center, “Federal Student Loan Portfolio.”
Loan Servicing and Repayment Topics
Various factors contributed to the rising delinquency and defaults on ED-held loans beginning in FY2024 Q1. This discussion focuses on factors related to loan servicing, an issue raised by some current news and research. Economic factors (e.g., college costs, general affordability issues) or borrower educational experiences are not discussed.
Extended Forbearance Policies
The FY2025 Q4 increase in defaults (sometimes referred to as a “default cliff”) has been linked to congressional and Administration forbearance policies established in response to and following the COVID-19 pandemic. After the payment pause and on-ramp policies ended, many borrowers may have become disconnected from their loan servicers and fallen out of the practice of making monthly loan payments. ED has also noted the higher risk of delinquency or default following prolonged periods of forbearance. 
Observers hypothesize that other forbearance policies may generate more loan defaults. Since July 2024, ED placed millions of borrowers enrolled in the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment plan in forbearance in response to litigation challenging ED’s authority to establish the plan. After a federal court vacated the SAVE plan, borrowers must enroll in a different repayment plan or be placed in a standard repayment plan. As with previous forbearances, observers argue that prolonged periods without borrowers making payments may increase the likelihood that they become delinquent or default. Furthermore, research indicates that borrowers in income-driven repayment (IDR) plans, which base monthly payments on income (e.g., the SAVE plan), have lower default rates relative to those in standard repayment plans. Thus, placing SAVE plan enrollees who fail to select an IDR plan into a standard repayment plan raises concerns about potential future defaults.
Loan Servicing Issues
Historical and seemingly ongoing issues encountered in the loan administration environment may impact a borrower’s ability to successfully repay their loans, which may lead to negative impacts on their credit history. For example, in 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reported that “loan servicers routinely made basic payment processing errors,” including misreporting payment amounts. Findings show that borrowers have received conflicting, confusing, or inaccurate information from their loan servicers, contributing to some inadvertent or mistaken delinquencies appearing on borrower credit reports.
ED directed the transfer of servicing rights among student loan servicers in 2023, which may have contributed to nearly 2 million credit reporting errors. CRAs allegedly were not informed of the transfer, which could have affected credit profiles. For example, a single debt might appear as two duplicate loans, portraying borrowers as carrying higher debt amounts. If a loan appears closed and a “new loan” opened, then borrowers’ credit histories may be incorrectly shortened. Some borrowers’ on-time credit histories may not properly carry forward during transfer. 
Finally, implementation of 2025 statutory changes made to the federal student loan programs (e.g., the repeal of some existing and the authorization of new loan repayment plans) may further complicate loan administration. 
Negative Credit Reporting Issues
ED servicers may report both favorable and negative (late) payment history to the private CRAs. Student loan delinquencies can reduce credit scores by more than 150 points, limiting borrowers’ future credit access. Similarly, negative payment information reported to the Credit Alert Verification Reporting System (CAIVRS), a federal database managed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, can also limit credit access for some borrowers. CAIVRS is used to screen applicants and track delinquencies and defaults for loans that were made or insured by federal agencies such as the Federal Housing Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Small Business Administration, and ED. Unlike private CRAs, CAIVRS includes only information about federally made or insured loans that are 90 days or more past due—or have defaulted. Only authorized loan originators and federal agencies, and not private CRAs, can access CAIVRS. A federal agency, for example, may report negative information to CAIVRS without notifying private CRAs, causing an individual to appear creditworthy based solely on a private credit inquiry. (Conversely, someone with past-due loans that have no federal guarantee will not appear in CAIVRS.) Notably, individuals must rely on approved lenders to view their CAIVRS status. Thus, if a borrower’s loan status is reported to CAIVRS by ED servicers without the borrower’s knowledge, they may discover the reporting to CAIVRS while applying for a federally guaranteed mortgage or small business loan. Consequently, after resolving issues with ED, some borrowers may still need to dispute inaccurate information.

On October 20, 2026, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a Notice of Order Regarding Exclusion and Removal of DeepSeek Products from Federal Civilian Executive Branch Information Technology Systems and Procurements in the Federal Register. This notice requires federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) departments and agencies to bar products made by DeepSeek—a firm headquartered in the People’s Republic of China (PRC)—from their networks and to remove any DeepSeek products that may have already been deployed. The DHS order follows a similar action made by the Department of Defense (DOD, which is “using a secondary Department of War designation,” under Executive Order 14347) on September 8, 2026. The Director of National Intelligence (DNI) issued a similar order concurrently with DHS. This In Focus discusses these actions and their implications related to supply chain security.
Overview of DeepSeek
Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd. (DeepSeek) is an artificial intelligence (AI) company located in the PRC. DeepSeek develops open-weight large language models (LLM), such as (the eponymously named) DeepSeek and DeepSeek-R1. 
DeepSeek’s AI products have been noted for their general and cost efficiency. While their models are not as powerful as U.S. models, DeepSeek’s models have cheaper token costs, can perform tasks quickly, and can be downloaded, hosted, and customized. Because of this price-to-performance advantage, some U.S. companies have adopted DeepSeek’s (and other PRC AI) models. 
The U.S. government issued warnings about the risks of PRC AI models and their adoption. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the National Security Agency (NSA) have said that DeepSeek and its peer companies have carried out large-scale distillation campaigns (e.g., the systemic querying of an AI model and using its responses without authorization to train another model) on U.S. models to develop their products. Further, the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST’s) Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) found that DeepSeek’s AI models are more prone to jailbreaking, more likely to follow malicious commands than U.S. models, and more often provided users with narratives consistent with messaging from the Communist Party of China (CPC). 
DeepSeek models are available to U.S. users through several pathways. They can be accessed directly from DeepSeek (e.g., from its mobile application) or through domestic cloud service providers and AI platforms, or it can be downloaded and run on a user’s hardware.
Select Legislative Actions on DeepSeek
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (enacted December 18, 2025) requires that DOD issue an exclusion and removal order for DeepSeek technologies. That order was issued on September 8, 2026. The Department of the Air Force issued an exclusion and removal order on July 10, 2025. 
The U.S. House of Representative’s Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (Select Committee on China) issued a report on risks from DeepSeek and the company’s actions to subvert U.S. policy on April 16, 2025. The House Committee on Science Space and Technology held a hearing on DeepSeek on April 8, 2025. 
Exclusion and Removal Order
The Federal Register notice for the DHS order on DeepSeek products includes a copy of Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 from July 24, 2026. It states that DeepSeek poses risks to the United States for several reasons:
The company is subject to PRC laws, including the 2017 cybersecurity law (which could allow the government to compel disclosure of sensitive information from DeepSeek).
Signing up for a DeepSeek account would require the collection of personally identifiable information (PII).
DeepSeek collects inputs and outputs, which could result in sensitive information being transmitted to U.S. adversaries.
Any information leaked through DeepSeek could be used, or combined and used, with other information for actionable intelligence against the United States.
DHS also raises concerns that DeepSeek’s applications (such as the aforementioned mobile application) are configured in ways that are insecure.
Because of these risks, federal departments and agencies are required to bar DeepSeek, its affiliated entities, and their products from procurements. Further, any previously acquired products must be immediately removed. This order extends to federal contractors and firms doing business with the prime contractor.
Agencies may petition CISA for an exception to this order. Further, CISA will assist agencies in implementing the order. The order suggests that it should be reviewed within a year and annually thereafter.
This is the first time that DHS has exercised its authority to issue exclusion and removal orders—a tool to mitigate supply chain risks at federal agencies.
Authority to Combat Technology Risks
The U.S. government has taken several actions since 2017 to address potential foreign cyber technology risks. In September 2017, DHS issued a Binding Operational Directive ordering the removal of Kaspersky-branded software products from federal agency use. In December 2017, Congress passed a statute codifying that directive. 
Recognizing that foreign adversaries may seek to use information and communications technology (ICT) supply chains to compromise organizations, Congress sought to create a repeatable process for restricting potentially dangerous ICT from federal agencies. A precursor bill was debated and passed in the Senate before being enacted as the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (Title II of the SECURE Technology Act of 2018). This act, among other actions, created the Federal Acquisition Security Council (FASC).
Federal Acquisition Security Council
The FASC is an interagency body that serves as a government-wide forum to identify, assess, and manage ICT supply chain risks to the federal government. It can recommend that federal agencies exclude particular entities and products from federal procurement because they pose an unacceptable risk to national security.
Per the FASC’s implementing rule, a senior official from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) chairs the FASC. Other members include the General Services Administration (GSA), DHS, CISA, the DNI, the National Counterintelligence and Security Center (NCSC), the Department of Justice (DOJ), the FBI, DOD, NSA, the Department of Commerce, and NIST. These agencies provide the council with procurement, cybersecurity, intelligence, law enforcement, national security, and technical expertise.
U.S. government agencies may refer cases to the FASC. The FASC may investigate such cases and coordinate across federal departments and agencies (not just FASC members) on the risk posed by the product or company, develop and recommend potential remedies to address those risks, and (if necessary) issue requirements for agencies to exclude certain vendors or products from federal networks and remove such vendors or products. 
Exclusion and removal orders are issued by DHS for the FCEB, DOD for the military, and the DNI for the intelligence community (IC). All three agencies need not coordinate combined orders. The first exclusion and removal orders issued under this authority were by DNI and DOD (almost a year apart) for Acronis—a cybersecurity firm. DHS issued a similar order on October 27, 2026.  
The recent orders against DeepSeek are the first time that all three agencies have issued similar orders in close succession and the first time that DHS has exercised this authority.  
Considerations for Congress
The exclusion and removal orders issued by DOD, DNI, and CISA may spark interest among policymakers on what further actions Congress may take to combat the threat from DeepSeek, other PRC firms, and cyber supply chain risk management in both the public and private sectors.
Congress may seek to conduct oversight. The DeepSeek orders provide Congress a case study on the efficacy and utility of the FASC. Congress may choose to ask the Comptroller General (GAO), or the inspectors general for DHS, DOD, and the IC to evaluate the FASC’s implementation of the DeepSeek order as well its broader operations, including processes for referrals, coordinating and evaluating risk across the interagency, and barriers to issuing orders. GAO has previously assessed the FASC’s establishment and DOD’s support. 
The FASC limits federal procurement but does not restrict nongovernmental access to and use of DeepSeek. Congress may choose to consider the extent to which the Federal Acquisition Regulation’s extension of prohibitions to contractors creates a broader disincentive for the private sector to adopt the barred companies. (For example, when Congress barred Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation telecommunications equipment from servicing the government, it served as a disincentive for wider adoption in the private sector.) Congress may also choose to consider whether a federal prohibition for a cloud service provider (CSP) that contracts with federal government extends to the nonfederal instances of the services that a CSP provides. 
Relatedly, Congress might evaluate the risks that DHS, DOD, and the DNI determined regarding DeepSeek products and consider whether broader U.S. use restrictions are needed. Congress might also assess whether other PRC firms or technologies also merit scrutiny. While the FASC can create vendor prohibitions for the federal government, other departments and agencies can act broadly across the economy. For example, the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 authorizes the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to prevent communications equipment that poses national security risks from being deployed on U.S. networks. The FCC implements this through its Covered List. Congress may choose to examine the extent to which the FASC and other federal agencies have sufficient authority to combat transnational security risks from technology (e.g., AI). 
While the FASC process seeks to protect the federal government against ICT supply chain threats through procurement policy, those same threats extend to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments; the private sector; academia; and other nongovernmental organizations. Congress could also assess whether new authorities are needed to ensure adequate identification, analysis, and mitigation of ICT supply chain risks across the nation and whether agencies can efficiently work on whole-of-government approaches to ICT supply chain security and threat mitigation.

api_metadata.summary:
On August 17, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed a new rule that would make some noncitizens ineligible for the portion of certain refundable tax credits that exceed the taxpayer’s income tax liability. It would do so by applying the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA; P.L. 104-193)—which makes certain noncitizens ineligible for federal public benefits—to certain tax credits. This In Focus describes the proposed change and examines its potential impacts on taxpayers and the federal budget. 
PRWORA Overview
Title IV of PRWORA was designed to create a “national policy with respect to welfare and immigration.” Enacted on August 22, 1996, PRWORA, as amended, generally restricts noncitizens’ eligibility for public benefits through its baseline eligibility rule: Non-qualified aliens are prohibited from receiving federal public benefits. (Alien is the term used in the Immigration and Nationality Act for any person who is not a citizen or national of the United States. In this report, the words alien and noncitizen are used interchangeably.)
Qualified aliens include lawful permanent residents, refugees, aliens granted parole for at least one year, aliens granted asylum or related relief, certain abused spouses and children, Cuban-Haitian entrants, and citizens of the Freely Associated States residing in the U.S. states and territories (8 U.S.C. §1641). Non-qualified aliens include unauthorized noncitizens as well as various classes of noncitizens granted temporary permission to remain in the United States. 
PRWORA defines federal public benefit to include “any retirement, welfare, health, disability ... or any other similar benefit for which payments or assistance are provided to an individual, household, or family eligibility unit by an agency of the United States or by appropriated funds of the United States” (8 U.S.C. §1611(c)(1)). Historically, tax credits have not been considered federal public benefits, and thus PRWORA’s noncitizen restrictions have not applied. Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) have proposed a new regulation that would define four refundable individual tax credits as federal public benefits under PRWORA. Thus, non-qualified aliens would be ineligible to receive the refundable portion of those credits. 
Tax Treatment of Noncitizens
The individual income tax applies to income “from whatever source derived” unless explicitly excluded in the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. Federal taxes that noncitizens may pay directly include income tax, as well as payroll taxes, which apply to wages and fund specific programs such as Social Security, Medicare Hospital Insurance, and unemployment insurance. Noncitizens may also pay state and local taxes and may indirectly pay other federal taxes, such as the corporate income tax and tariffs, to the extent such taxes impact the noncitizens’ incomes or consumer prices. 
Noncitizens may be subject to U.S. income taxes when, for example, they work in the United States. Similarly, payroll taxes typically apply to the wages of all U.S. employees, which generally include noncitizens working in the United States (with some exceptions).
Noncitizens can claim credits against their income tax liability unless expressly prohibited by law. Statute prohibits some taxpayers from claiming certain credits if they do not have work-authorized Social Security numbers (SSNs). Such credits include the Child Tax Credit (CTC), the Earned Income Tax credit (EITC), and the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC). 
Noncitizen Eligibility for Work-Authorized SSNs
Noncitizens with current employment authorization from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) may obtain SSNs that indicate their employment authorization status at the time of their SSN applications. This is known as a “work-authorized SSN.” Work-authorized SSNs do not expire and may not indicate current citizenship, immigration, or employment authorization status. There are various types of work authorization, and a noncitizen may be issued an Unrestricted SSN Card or a Work SSN Card that is valid only with DHS work authorization. 

While possession of an SSN is sometimes used as a proxy for lawful immigration status, it is not an exact one. Someone in a household that files a tax return may be in the country lawfully on a nonimmigrant visa but is not eligible to work (and thus not eligible for a work-authorized SSN) because he or she is a spouse or child of the principal visa holder. Others without work-authorized SSNs may be unlawfully present in the country, using Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers instead of SSNs. Conversely, some unlawfully present noncitizens may file using work-authorized SSNs they lawfully received in the past (e.g., they may have been lawfully present and authorized to work but overstayed their authorized period of admission). Some people may also use work-authorized SSNs obtained fraudulently. 
Proposed Rule
On August 19, 2026, Treasury released a new proposed rule that would deem the refundable portion of certain tax credits to be federal public benefits under PRWORA. The refundable portion of a tax credit is the portion paid to a taxpayer in excess of tax liability. The tax credits that the rule would impact are 
the CTC, which is worth a maximum of $2,200 per qualifying child but for which $1,700 per child can be received as a tax refund; 
the EITC, a fully refundable tax credit that subsidizes the wages of low- and moderate-income workers, particularly those with children; 
the adoption tax credit, which offsets up to $17,280 (2026 value; adjusted annually for inflation) in qualifying expenses related to the adoption of a child, of which up to $5,000 (not adjusted for inflation) can be received as a tax refund; and 
the AOTC, which offsets up to $2,500 of a household’s expenses on higher education per qualifying student, of which up to $1,000 per student can be received as a tax refund. 
Existing statute requires taxpayers to have work-authorized SSNs to claim the CTC, the EITC, or the AOTC. Filers claiming the CTC must provide work-authorized SSNs for either themselves or their spouses (if filing jointly) as well as the children for whom they are claiming the credit. In contrast, for the EITC, a work-authorized SSN is required for the taxpayer, a spouse if married filing jointly, and any children for whom the taxpayer is claiming the credit. Those claiming the AOTC must provide work-authorized SSNs for themselves and the eligible students for whom they are claiming the credit, unless such student is the taxpayer’s spouse. No such requirement exists for the adoption tax credit. 
The proposed rule applies to only the refundable portion of these credits, meaning the portion that exceeds the amount of income tax liability. Therefore, it changes credit eligibility for non-qualified aliens with no income tax liability after claiming credits. Such aliens may still have federal payroll tax liability, which generally does not factor into the calculation of the refundable portion of a tax credit. Payroll tax liability generally applies to the first dollar a worker earns in wages or salary, without deductions or credits, meaning working taxpayers with no income tax liability generally have payroll tax liability. 
Potential Impact of the Proposed Rule
The proposed rule reduces the value of credits for non-qualified aliens who claim refundable tax credits that exceed their income tax liability and who meet the work-authorized SSN requirements that apply to the credits. Such taxpayers would include all non-qualified aliens claiming the refundable portion of the adoption tax credit. They also include non-qualified aliens claiming the refundable portion of the CTC, EITC, or AOTC whose claims meet the applicable SSN requirements for such credits. Those who do not otherwise meet the SSN requirements for these credits are already ineligible. 
The IRS estimates that the rule would make 200,000 to 700,000 filers (representing 0.8% to 2.8% of all taxpayers) ineligible for the credits in 2026. Because filing units contain both taxpayers and other individuals, such as children, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimated that the changes to the CTC and EITC (the two largest affected credits) would impact roughly 1 million individuals (including U.S. citizen family members). 
Because those whose credits exceed their income tax liability are generally lower-income taxpayers, this rule would reduce the financial resources of lower-earning households more than moderate or higher earning ones. Households with workers would also be affected disproportionately, as the CTC and EITC both phase in with a taxpayer’s earned income and are thus already unavailable to those with no earned income. Households with children or other dependents are more likely to otherwise qualify for the affected credits—or qualify for larger credits—and therefore would be disproportionately affected by the rule. 
Requiring taxpayers to affirm that they are qualified aliens (or otherwise eligible under PROWRA) on their tax returns may add an administrative burden to taxpayers, who may need to research the definition of qualified alien to make their claims. It could also dissuade some from filing their income taxes and claiming benefits or refunds to which they are entitled out of concern that the information will be used against them in immigration enforcement. While the IRS has not historically collected information on immigration enforcement or shared information systematically with enforcement agencies, last year it agreed to share tax return information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which uses the shared information to cross-reference individuals’ identifying information for enforcement purposes. Legal challenges to this arrangement are delaying its implementation. 
The rule could make households ineligible for state tax credits as well as these federal ones. Many states offer tax credits, such as state-level CTCs and earned income credits, with parameters that conform to the parameters of these federal credits in some ways. For example, 32 states and the District of Columbia offer state earned income credits, and all but three determine the state credit as a percentage of the federal EITC. Making non-qualified aliens ineligible for the refundable portion of the federal EITC could thus reduce the amount of state credits for which they are eligible. 
Implementation
The comment period for the proposed regulations closed on October 5, 2026. The IRS has not announced when it intends to issue final regulations.
The IRS has released a draft of a new form, Schedule 3-A of Form 1040, on which taxpayers claiming the refundable portions of these four credits would affirm that they (or their spouses) are either U.S. citizens or qualified aliens for purposes of PROWRA. Such a form is necessary because historically the IRS has not collected information on the immigration status of taxpayers as part of the standard individual income tax filing process. The new form is in addition to a question on the IRS’s draft of the Form 1040 itself for the 2026 tax year, which would ask all filers whether they (and their spouses, if filing jointly) are U.S. citizens, nationals, or aliens lawfully authorized to work in the United States.

relatedMaterials.title: To allow a period in which members of the clergy may revoke their exemption from Social Security coverage, and for other purposes.

api_metadata.summary:
Background
Social Security is a federal insurance program that provides monthly cash benefits to workers and their eligible family members in the event of a worker’s retirement, disability, or death. A worker’s employment or self-employment is considered covered by Social Security when the resulting earnings are taxable and creditable for program purposes. Although participation in Social Security is compulsory for most workers, about 6% of all workers in paid employment or self-employment are not covered by Social Security and are not subject to its payroll tax, including certain members of the clergy.
Congress has periodically provided clergy members with limited opportunities to revoke a previously granted exemption from Social Security taxes and elect coverage under the program. Most recently, the Clergy Act (P.L. 119-125), signed into law on October 20, 2026, established another opportunity for eligible clergy members to revoke their exemptions from Social Security taxes. This In Focus examines Social Security coverage for clergy members, the potential benefits and tax implications of electing coverage, and the provisions and estimated budgetary effects of the Clergy Act. 
Social Security and Medicare Taxes
In 2026, an estimated 185 million workers will pay into Social Security via Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) taxes, Self-Employment Contributions Act (SECA) taxes, or both on their covered wages and self-employment income. Both employers and employees contribute payroll taxes at the FICA rate, and the self-employed pay SECA taxes. 
Both payroll taxes have three components: Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and the Hospital Insurance (HI) part of Medicare (see Table 1). The OASDI (combined OASI and DI) payroll tax is levied on covered earnings up to $184,500 in 2026. The HI payroll tax is levied on all covered earnings.
Table 1. Current-Law Social Security and Medicare Tax Rates 
Tax Rates as a Percentage of Taxable Earnings


Rate for Employees and Employers, Each (FICA)

OASDI
6.20%

HIa

Total
7.65%

Rate for Self-Employed Workers (SECA)b

Source: Social Security Administration, “Social Security and Medicare Tax Rates,” https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/ProgData/taxRates.html. 
Notes: FICA = Federal Insurance Contributions Act; SECA = Self-Employment Contributions Act; OASDI = Old Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance; and HI = Hospital Insurance (Medicare Part A).
Beginning in 2013, individuals with earned income of more than $200,000 ($250,000 for married couples filing jointly) pay an additional 0.9% in Medicare taxes, which is not reflected in the tax rates shown in the table. 
Certain adjustments and income tax deductions apply. 
Social Security Coverage for Clergy Members
Ministers, members of religious orders who have not taken a vow of poverty, Christian Science practitioners, and members of recognized religious sects (such as the Amish and Mennonites) are automatically covered by Social Security as self-employed workers, and thus subject to SECA taxes. However, they may file for an exemption (generally irrevocable) with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) on the grounds of conscience or religious principle. The application for an exemption must be filed no later than the due date of the tax return for the second taxable year in which the clergy member earns wages for ministerial services (26 U.S.C. §1402 (e)(3)).
Members of religious orders who have taken a vow of poverty are not automatically covered by Social Security and are therefore exempt from paying SECA taxes on earnings from ministerial services performed as agents of their church or its agencies. However, the religious order may elect Social Security coverage for its vow-of-poverty members by filing a request with the IRS. For more information, see IRS, Pub. 517 (2026), Social Security and Other Information for Members of the Clergy and Religious Workers.
Past Legislative Provisions to Reverse the SECA Tax Exemption
By law, clergy members must apply for an exemption from SECA taxes early in their ministerial careers, and once granted, the exemption is generally irrevocable. Consequently, clergy members who obtain an exemption early in their careers may face challenges in preparing for retirement later in life. To address this issue, Congress has provided time-limited opportunities for clergy members to revoke their exemptions from SECA taxes.
Congress has provided three opportunities previously to revoke the SECA tax exemption before 2026: the Social Security Amendments of 1977 (P.L. 95-216 §316), the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (P.L. 99-514 §1704(b)), and the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 (P.L. 106-170 §403). Table 2 summarizes the time frames established under each law during which clergy members could elect to revoke their exemption from Social Security coverage. Outside these designated periods, revocation has not been permitted. Once a clergy member revokes the exemption, the ministerial earnings in the specified taxable year and any year afterwards are subject to SECA taxes. The decision to elect Social Security coverage is irrevocable, and the individual may not subsequently apply for an exemption from Social Security coverage.
Table 2. Legislative Provisions Revoking the Self-Employment Contributions Act (SECA) Tax Exemption for Clergy Members Before 2026
Legislation
Time Frame to File Revocation 

The Social Security Amendments of 1977 (P.L. 95-216)From the date of enactment (December 20, 1977) to the due date of the federal income tax return for the first taxable year beginning after the enactment date (generally April 16, 1979, but could be later with extensions).

The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (P.L. 99-514)From the date of enactment (October 22, 1986) to the due date of the federal income tax return for the first taxable year beginning after the enactment date (generally April 15, 1988, but could be later with extensions).
The Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 (P.L. 106-170).From the date of enactment (December 17, 1999) to the due date of the federal income tax return for the second taxable year beginning after December 31, 1999 (generally April 15, 2002, but could be later with extensions).

Source: Congressional Research Service. 
Note: Under each act, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) had to set up a process for clergy members to file the revocation, which typically took several months. For example, to implement the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999, the IRS released the relevant form (Form 2031) in April 2000. 
Social Security Benefits for Clergy Members
Workers become eligible for Social Security benefits for themselves and their family members through employment covered by Social Security. To qualify for Social Security retired-worker benefits, a worker generally must earn 40 credits, equivalent to 10 years of covered employment. Fewer credits are required to qualify for Social Security disability benefits, with the number varying according to the worker’s age at the onset of disability. A worker’s initial monthly benefit amount is based on average earnings over his or her career in covered employment. For example, retired-worker benefits are calculated using the worker’s 35 years of highest indexed covered earnings.
Clergy members who elect Social Security coverage generally need 10 years of covered employment to qualify for retired-worker benefits. Earnings from nonministerial work covered by Social Security also count toward this requirement. In general, workers with more years of covered earnings may receive higher initial monthly benefits because additional earnings are included in the benefit calculation.
Clergy members with no or limited Social Security-covered earnings may qualify for auxiliary benefits based on another individual’s earnings record. These benefits may be payable to eligible spouses, former spouses, survivors, children, or parents of a worker covered by Social Security.
Social Security Windfall Elimination Provision (WEP)
From 1984 through 2023, clergy members’ Social Security benefits could have been reduced by the WEP if they had earnings from both Social Security-covered and noncovered employment and received pension benefits based on their noncovered earnings. The Social Security Fairness Act of 2023 (P.L. 118-273) repealed the WEP and the Government Pension Offset for monthly benefits payable after December 2023. Accordingly, beginning in 2024, the WEP no longer applies to Social Security benefits, including those received by clergy members who elected Social Security coverage.

The Clergy Act (H.R. 227)
The Clergy Act (P.L. 119-125), signed into law on October 20, 2026, provides clergy members with another limited opportunity to revoke a previously elected exemption from SECA taxes. Eligible clergy members may revoke their exemptions by filing a revocation during the period beginning after enactment (subject to the IRS’s implementation process) and ending on the due date of their federal income tax return for their second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028 (expected to generally be April 15, 2031, but could be different with extensions or changes). The revocation may take effect in either the 2029 or 2030 tax year as specified in the application. Once effective, the revocation is irrevocable. The act also directs the IRS to develop a plan to notify eligible clergy members of this opportunity, helping ensure they are aware of their ability to participate in Social Security and potentially qualify for related retirement benefits.
Clergy members who revoke their exemptions will pay SECA taxes on their ministerial earnings for the remainder of their working years and may subsequently qualify for Social Security and Medicare benefits. Additional years of covered earnings may also increase their Social Security benefits. As a result, the law is expected to increase revenues (and thus reduce federal deficits) in the near term and increase outlays (and thus increase federal deficits) in later decades.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that approximately 3,000 clergy members would reverse their decisions in 2029 or 2030, resulting in an $84 million increase in payroll tax revenues over the 2026-2036 period. Of that amount, an estimated $68 million would come from additional Social Security payroll taxes and $16 million from additional Medicare payroll taxes. 
CBO estimates that outlays for Social Security and Medicare benefits would each increase by $1 million over the 2026-2036 period as a result of those reversals. Most of the additional benefits attributable to the reversals would be paid after 2036.
CBO also estimates that implementing the legislation, including reporting to Congress on efforts to inform clergy members about their eligibility to elect coverage, would increase the IRS’s administrative costs by less than $500,000. Such spending would be subject to the availability of appropriated funds.
