relatedMaterials.title: Allowing Emancipation Hall to be used for a ceremony to dedicate the Semiquincentennial Congressional Time Capsule on Wednesday, June 24, 2026.

api_metadata.summary:
On July 4, 2026, the United States celebrated the semiquincentennial (250th) anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. As part of the celebration, Congress authorized two time capsules—one for Philadelphia, PA, to be placed near Independence Hall, and one for Washington, DC, to be placed in the U.S. Capitol. In addition to these authorizations, this In Focus also discusses past official time capsules to celebrate milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence.
Over the ages, time capsules have captured the popular mind ... Time capsules are about sending out slices of our time to the future. 
All successful time capsules must evoke ... a real sense of immediacy with a given period of historical-cultural space-time, supplied by a wide variety of significant human details, mundane, grandiose or both.
—William E. Jarvis, Time Capsules: A Cultural History 
(McFarland & Co., 2003), pp. 2, 16.
Semiquincentennial Time Capsules
To celebrate the semiquincentennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Congress authorized two capsules—one in Philadelphia, PA and one in Washington, DC.
Philadelphia Time Capsule
In 2016, Congress authorized the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission (America250) to create a time capsule containing “a representative portion of all books, manuscripts, miscellaneous printed matter, memorabilia, relics, and other materials relating to the United States Semiquincentennial,” to be buried on Independence Mall on July 4, 2026, and unearthed on the 500th anniversary of the United States on July 4, 2276 (P.L. 114-196, §7(f)). 
“America’s Time Capsule” was built by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and was buried on July 4, 2026, at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia. The semiquincentennial time capsule contains submissions from each state, the District of Columbia, and each territory. Other submissions originate from America250 and its partner organizations, including the International Olympic Committee and NBC’s TODAY Show, the Library of Congress, Major League Baseball, the National Basketball Association, the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Football League, the National Hockey League, NIST, the Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) of America and the PGA Tour, the Smithsonian Institution, and the Supreme Court of the United States. Figure 1 shows “America’s Time Capsule” at the burial ceremony in Philadelphia, PA.
Figure 1. America’s Time Capsule, Philadelphia
/
Source: America250, “America250 Time Capsule,” July 5, 2026.
Congressional Time Capsule
In 2026, Congress authorized the creation of a time capsule and its burial in the U.S. Capitol Visitor Center (P.L. 119-79). The time capsule was unveiled on June 24, 2026, and put on display in Emancipation Hall (H.Con.Res. 109). At the ceremony, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson noted that “In many ways, the Congressional Time Capsule is a reflection of our faith in the future of this grand experiment in self-governance, faith that this moment is worth preserving, and faith that the great American story will endure for another 250 years.”
The Congressional Time Capsule’s legislation (P.L. 119-79) specified that the capsule is to include “a single, joint letter” from congressional leadership and any other item that leadership jointly determines appropriate. The Architect of the Capitol issued a series of Dear Colleague letters about contents of the time capsule. For a list of contributions from congressional delegations, see https://www.visitthecapitol.gov/tc-kiosk-embed. Specific burial plans for the Congressional Time Capsule have yet to be announced. The time capsule is scheduled to be opened on July 4, 2276, during the 244th Congress (P.L. 119-79, §2(d)). Figure 2 shows the Congressional Time Capsule on display in Emancipation Hall of the Capitol Visitor Center. 
Figure 2. Congressional Time Capsule, U.S. Capitol Visitor Center
/
Source: U.S. Capitol (@visitthecapitol), X post, July 23, 2026.
Past Anniversary Time Capsules
At least two previous milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence involved time capsules as part of the celebration—for the 1876 centennial and the 1976 bicentennial.
Centennial (1876)
In 1876, Philadelphia hosted the Centennial Exhibition to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. For the 1876 Centennial Exposition, Mrs. Anna Deihm, widow of Civil War veteran Charles F. Deihm, facilitated the creation of a safe to be filled with memorabilia from the centennial celebrations. In 1879, Deihm offered the safe as a gift to the United States, with the expectation that it would be opened in 1976 by the President of the United States. In February 1879, Congress held a ceremony in the Capitol to formally close the safe. On January 19, 1976, at the beginning of the 2nd session of the 94th Congress (1975-1976), Representatives and Senators attended a ceremony to open the outer doors of the safe, which was then put on display for public viewing. Figure 3 shows the Centennial Safe as opened by President Ford in 1976.
Figure 3. Centennial Safe
/
Source: Warren K. Leffler, Mrs. Charles F. Deihm’s “Centennial Safe” Kept at the U.S. Capitol and Opened by President Gerald Ford as Part of the United States Bicentennial, photograph, Library of Congress, June 23, 1976.
Bicentennial (1976)
For the bicentennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the congressionally authorized American Revolution Bicentennial Administration (P.L. 93-179) created the National Bicentennial Time Capsule “as a bicentennial gift to the United States.” The National Bicentennial Time Capsule was 1 of 56 time capsules made by the Reynolds Metals Company, which, according to media reports, gave one to each state and territory. The National Bicentennial Time Capsule is stored by the National Archives and Records Administration and is scheduled to be opened on July 4, 2075. Figure 4 shows the National Bicentennial Time Capsule.
Figure 4. National Bicentennial Time Capsule
/
Source: American Revolution Bicentennial Administration, “National Bicentennial Time Capsule,” National Archives and Records Administration, 1976.
For more information on congressional celebrations of milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence, see CRS Report R48473, Congressional Involvement in the Celebration of Anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence, by Jacob R. Straus.

State Proposals to Change Daylight Saving Time Observance
Daylight saving time (DST) is a period of the year between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time (ST). The United States first adopted DST in 1918. DST begins on the second Sunday in March and ends on the first Sunday in November. The beginning and end dates are set in statute (15 U.S.C. §260a). 
Congressional interest in the potential benefits and costs of DST has resulted in changes to DST observance (including changes to its start and end dates, periods of temporary year-round DST, and periods of no federal DST observance). Though the authority to change DST observance rests solely with Congress, since 2015, a majority of states have had legislation introduced to change the observance of DST—seeking to establish either DST or ST year round. State-enacted permanent DST would go into effect if and when such action is allowed by Congress.

Forty-seven states and DC have had legislation introduced proposing some variation of permanent year-round DST. 
* Introduced permanent DST
* Enacted permanent DST (19 states)
* Adopted nonbinding resolution in support of permanent DST
* No DST legislation introduced
Forty-two states have had legislation introduced to establish permanent year-round ST. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 as amended (15 U.S.C. §§260-267) allows states to exempt themselves from observing DST.
* Introduced permanent ST 
* No ST legislation introduced
* Observes permanent ST 

Sources: State legislation information from Lexis Advance “Statutes and Legislation” database; state legislature websites/databases; National Council of State Legislature’s Daylight Saving Time | State Legislation resource; CQ.com’s Policy Note database. 
Notes: American Samoa, most of Arizona, Guam, Hawaii, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands do not observe DST. CRS identified introduced legislation from January 2015 to August 2026 that would amend time observance; in this search, CRS did not identify any introduced legislation for the U.S. territories that would amend time observance. 
For more information, see CRS Report R45208, Daylight Saving Time (DST).
Information as of October 19, 2026. Prepared by Corrie E. Clark, Specialist in Energy Policy; Lynn J. Cunningham, Senior Research Librarian; Cassandra E. Higgins, Geospatial Information Systems Analyst; and Amber Wilhelm, Visual Information Specialist.

The Senate’s unique procedural rules have long been a source of interest both inside and outside of Congress. While some hold the view that Senate rules operate well, others have advocated an examination of Senate procedures with an eye toward changing them. This Insight highlights eight parliamentary mechanisms that might be used to implement procedural change in the Senate and links to additional reading material on the subject.
The work of the U.S. Senate is regulated not just by its 44 standing rules but by multiple, sometimes overlapping, procedural authorities. At any given time, unanimous consent agreements, standing orders, statute, precedent, and provisions of the U.S. Constitution may also regulate the Senate as it processes its legislative and executive business. It is perhaps natural for those seeking changes to Senate procedures to think in terms of “amending Senate rules,” but directly amending the standing rules of the Senate is only one way to affect chamber procedures. Because some Senate actions are, or may be, controlled by multiple authorities, it is sometimes possible to achieve the same procedural outcome using more than one parliamentary mechanism. While each mechanism may achieve identical ends, each may also have procedural advantages and disadvantages that make it a more or less desirable path for action in a given instance. Here are eight such mechanisms:
Amend the standing rules. Because the Senate is a “continuing body,” its standing rules remain in force from Congress to Congress unless changed. A motion to proceed to consider a resolution (S.Res.) reported by a committee directly amending the Senate’s standing rules is always debatable and requires one day’s written notice. If a unanimous consent request for the immediate consideration of a resolution amending the standing rules is objected to, the resolution “goes over, under the rule” and is placed in a parliamentary status from which it is difficult to retrieve. Although agreeing to a rules change resolution requires only a majority vote, invoking cloture on such a resolution (which is fully debatable and subject to amendment) requires a vote of two-thirds of Senators present and voting, with a quorum present—67 if all Senators vote. It appears the same cloture threshold would likely apply to the motion to proceed to such a resolution. Direct amendments to the standing rules are also occasionally made by statute.
Create or amend a standing order. The Senate sometimes instead establishes chamber procedures by standing order. Standing orders have the same force as standing rules but are not codified in the rules. The Senate Manual lists major standing orders now in force. Standing orders continue in effect until changed, unless the order specifies otherwise. They are frequently established by resolution but can also be ordered by unanimous consent. A motion to proceed to consider a reported resolution establishing a standing order is debatable, and invoking cloture on that motion, and on the measure itself, requires a three-fifths vote of the Senate—60 votes if there is not more than one vacancy—a lower threshold than required for cloture on resolutions proposing direct amendments to the standing rules. 
Unanimous consent. More than any other parliamentary mechanism, the Senate uses unanimous consent agreements to process and establish the terms for considering floor business. Senate Rule V provides that any rule may be suspended without notice by unanimous consent unless the rules specify otherwise. Any Senator present on the floor when a consent request is propounded can object, including on another Senator’s behalf, blocking the request. Once agreed to, a unanimous consent agreement may be subsequently altered in whole or in part by another such consent agreement. 
Establish a new precedent. Senate procedural actions are also regulated by parliamentary precedent. Rulings of the presiding officer on the application of chamber rules are generally subject to an appeal to the full Senate. In most procedural circumstances, appeals are debatable. This fact operates as a significant bar to creating new precedent by appeal. When appeals are made in procedural circumstances that render them nondebatable, however—for example, after cloture has been invoked or when the appeal is made in relation to a nondebatable motion—no supermajority to limit debate is needed, and a majority can overrule the chair and establish a new understanding of what a Senate rule means or how it is applied. 
Enact a rulemaking statute. The Senate sometimes enacts parliamentary rules in law, such as the Congressional Review Act and the Trade Act of 1974. Doing so requires two-chamber passage of a bill or joint resolution and presidential approval (or veto override). Rules changes might appear in a bill as introduced or be added by amendment. Calling up and reaching a final vote on legislation may each require a three-fifths vote for cloture except if the measure directly amends the Senate’s standing rules, in which case a two-thirds vote is necessary.
Suspend the rules. Rule V also makes in order a motion to suspend Senate rules, including rules in law, such as the Congressional Budget Act. A motion to suspend the rules does not permanently change Senate rules; it suspends them only in the specific case and in the exact manner specified in the motion. The motion to suspend requires one day’s written notice before consideration, and its adoption is by a two-thirds vote, a quorum being present. Such motions are debatable, and a three-fifths cloture vote may be necessary to reach a final vote. Under a 2011 precedent, motions to suspend the rules are not in order postcloture.
Amend the Constitution. The Constitution establishes certain parliamentary rules for the Senate, including its business quorum and the requirement to maintain a journal. A constitutional amendment may be proposed by Congress by a two-thirds vote of each chamber or by a constitutional convention called for by two-thirds of the state legislatures. Such an amendment becomes part of the Constitution once ratified by three-fourths of the states. Joint resolutions proposing constitutional amendments are debatable and amendable. Successfully calling up such a measure and reaching a vote on it in the Senate could both require three-fifths vote for cloture. 
Voluntary action. Significant procedural change can sometimes occur as a result of voluntary action undertaken by Senate leaders or groups of Senators acting collectively. In 2011, for example, Senate leaders entered into a voluntary informal agreement related to extended debate and the offering of floor amendments. Such “gentlemen’s agreements” are not procedurally enforceable, however.  
For additional reading on mechanisms to change Senate procedures and recent related actions, see:
CRS Report R42929, Procedures for Considering Changes in Senate Rules;
CRS Report R41342, Proposals to Change the Operation of Cloture in the Senate;
CRS Report R44395, Amending Senate Rules at the Start of a New Congress, 1953-1975: An Analysis with an Afterword to 2015;
CRS Report R42928, “First Day” Proceedings and Procedural Change in the Senate;
CRS Report R42996, Changes to Senate Procedures at the Start of the 113th Congress Affecting the Operation of Cloture (S.Res. 15 and S.Res. 16); and
CRS Report R43331, Majority Cloture for Nominations: Implications and the “Nuclear” Proceedings of November 21, 2013.

api_metadata.summary:
Immigration courts within the Department of Justice’s (DOJ’s) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) are responsible for adjudicating proceedings to determine whether an alien (referred to as the respondent) may be removed from the United States. During these removal proceedings, respondents have the right to certain procedural protections found in the Immigration and Nationality Act, including “the privilege of being represented, at no expense to the Government, by counsel of the alien’s choosing who is authorized to practice in such proceedings.” That is, respondents may obtain counsel, either at their own expense or by obtaining the services of the pro bono bar, but the federal government generally may not fund or appoint counsel. 
Many respondents do not have representation in removal proceedings. Beginning with pilot programs in detention facilities in the 1990s, EOIR has funded programs that offer legal orientations and other services to unrepresented respondents to improve efficiency in removal proceedings. Congress has appropriated funds for such programs since the early 2000s. In FY2024, Congress appropriated $28 million to the Legal Orientation Program. A full-year continuing resolution for FY2025 (P.L. 119-4) continued to fund EOIR at FY2024 levels and subject to the same conditions.
Until recently, EOIR’s Office of Legal Access Programs (OLAP) offered several initiatives that facilitated access to legal information and referrals, and these initiatives were administered by a contracted organization—most recently, the Acacia Center for Justice (Acacia)—that subcontracted with nonprofit legal service providers. Programs included the following:
Legal Orientation Program (LOP), established in 2003, which provided legal orientation and workshops and pro bono referrals for adults in immigration detention facilities;
Legal Orientation Program for Custodians (LOPC), established in 2010, which provided legal orientation for the adult caregivers of unaccompanied alien children (UAC) in removal proceedings;
Immigration Court Helpdesk (ICH), established in 2016, which provided legal orientations, workshops, pro bono referrals, and friend of the court services to non-detained respondents; 
Counsel for Children Initiative (CCI), established in 2021, which provided representation for certain UAC;
Family Group Legal Orientation Program (FGLOP) for certain families, established in 2021; 
Legal Access Services for Reunified Families (LASRF) Program for individuals covered as class members and qualifying additional family members under a settlement agreement reached in 2023 in Ms. L v. ICE, a class action suit involving a legal challenge relating to the separation of alien parents and children at the Southwest border; and
the National Qualified Representative Program (NQRP), established in 2013, which provided representation to detained individuals who were found by an immigration judge or the Board of Immigration Appeals (EOIR’s appellate body) to be incompetent to represent themselves in proceedings. The program followed a court order entered by a U.S. district court judge in Franco-Gonzalez v. Holder, after finding that, under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (P.L. 93-112), individuals with serious mental disorders are entitled to a qualified representative as a reasonable accommodation during removal proceedings. Although the Franco order applied to a limited certified class, EOIR implemented NQRP as a nationwide program. 
Acacia reported that in January 2025, DOJ issued a stop work order pausing the LOP, ICH, FGLOP, and CCI. The order followed Executive Order 14159, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” Section 19 of the order directs the Attorney General and Secretary of Homeland Security to review contracts and grants that provide federal funding to nongovernmental organizations that provide services to “removable or illegal aliens,” “pause distribution of all further funds” under review, terminate agreements and prohibit future agreements “determined to be in violation of law or to be sources of waste, fraud, or abuse,” and ensure that such funding is not included in appropriations requests.
In January 2025, a group of legal services providers filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking to block DOJ from terminating the programs, and it was reported that DOJ rescinded the stop work order in early February 2025. On April 3, 2025, DOJ sent Acacia a Notice of Termination for Convenience terminating contracts associated with LOP, FGLOP, LOPC, CCI, ICH, NQRP, and LASRF, stating that such services were “no longer needed” and should be discontinued. On April 10, Acacia received notice from DOJ that it was terminating task orders for FGLOP, CCI, ICH, LOP, and LOPC, effective April 16. DOJ cited Federal Acquisition Regulations that permit the government to terminate government contracted work when the “termination is in the Government’s interest.” The court issued a judgment in favor of DOJ on July 6, 2025, concluding, in part, that the court lacked jurisdiction to review the plaintiffs’ claims, and otherwise rejecting their claims on the merits. The legal service providers are appealing the ruling.
DOJ also limited the scope of the NQRP. On April 25, 2025, DOJ submitted to Acacia a revised Statement of Work stating that NQRP is “limited to class members covered by Franco,” ending its designation as a nationwide program. Legal services organizations filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and sought a preliminary injunction asking the court to prohibit the termination of the NQRP nationwide. DOJ moved to dismiss, arguing that the court lacks jurisdiction to review the plaintiffs’ claims. On July 21, 2025, the district court judge granted plaintiff’s request for preliminary relief, blocking DOJ from terminating the program.  
Additionally, on June 10, 2025, following DOJ’s termination of its contract with Acacia for legal access services under the LASRF program, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California in the Ms. L v. ICE litigation mentioned above granted the plaintiffs’ motion to enforce the class action settlement agreement in that case, which requires the provision of legal access services to class members.
In DOJ’s FY2026 budget request, EOIR has requested that Congress remove statutory language regarding LOP funding in its appropriation. Its former OLAP website has been replaced by a Public Resources Program website, which includes information about NQRP and LASRF.

Acknowledgements
CRS Research Librarian Tilly Finnegan-Kennel provided research support for this Insight.

api_metadata.summary:
On Friday, August 1, 2025, President Trump sent dismissal notices to five of the seven members of Puerto Rico’s Financial Oversight and Management Board (FOMB or Oversight Board): Arthur J. Gonzalez, Cameron McKenzie, Betty A. Rosa, Juan A. Sabater, and Luis A. Ubiñas. On August 13, 2025, a week after these dismissals, FOMB member Andrew G. Biggs described them as a “setback for Puerto Rico.” He then also received a notice of dismissal from the White House, according to an Oversight Board statement. John E. Nixon is the sole member of the Oversight Board who did not receive a dismissal notice.
On September 18, 2025, Gonzalez, Rosa, and Biggs sued to challenge their dismissals, contending that “in violation of the statutory text, Judge Gonzalez, Dr. Biggs, and Dr. Rosa were purportedly terminated without cause, as the emails provided no basis, justification, or authority for the terminations.” On October 3, 2025, federal district court judge María Antongiorgi-Jordán granted a preliminary injunction, holding that the board members “have never been properly removed from office,” and barred officials from “effectuating in any manner the attempted removal of Plaintiffs from their positions.” On December 2, 2025, defendants filed an appeal.
That appeal was stayed pending the Supreme Court’s consideration of a potentially related case and, after the Supreme Court ruled in that matter, remanded to the district court at defendants’ request. On September 1, 2026, the district court converted the preliminary injunction into a permanent one. The Trump Administration did not object to this action, but indicated that it understood the order as focused on the alleged lack of process provided in the removals and not precluding “any future removals of Plaintiffs consistent with law.”
The Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA; P.L. 114-187), enacted in June 2016, established the Oversight Board and created processes for restructuring Puerto Rico’s public debts, among other provisions. PROMESA Title III established a bankruptcy-like process that has been used for most debt restructuring cases. Title VI established a process similar to sovereign debt workout procedures.
How Are Board Members Appointed?
Members, including those purportedly terminated, are appointed through a process established in Section 101(e) of PROMESA. In that process, six of the seven board members are appointed by the President from lists submitted by congressional leaders. For the original members, the Speaker and the Senate Majority Leader each submitted two lists for the appointments of two members (four members total). The House Minority Leader and the Senate Minority Leader each submitted one list for one appointment. The President appointed a seventh member at his sole discretion. Each Oversight Board vacancy thereafter is filled in the same manner in which the original member was appointed.
PROMESA (48 U.S.C. §2121) also allows the President to send board member nominations to the Senate for confirmation. Thus, if the President chooses to fill a vacancy via Senate confirmation, he need not select from a list.
Four of the Oversight Board members who received dismissal notices, according to media reports, were nominated by Democratic leaders. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries nominated former chair of the board Arthur Gonzalez for his latest appointment. Then-Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had put forward Betty Rosa and Luis Ubiñas. President Biden had used his discretion to appoint Juan Sabater, and Speaker Mike Johnson nominated Cameron McKenzie. Then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell put forward Andrew Biggs in 2016 and for reappointment in 2020.
Issues Regarding Attempted Dismissals of Board Members
PROMESA authorizes the President to remove members “only for cause” (48 U.S.C. §2121(e)(5)(B)). The August 2025 dismissal notices sent to Oversight Board members, quoted in legal filings, articulated no cause. The Administration sent letters to those members on September 26, 2025, alleging “inefficiency, ineffectiveness, neglect, and failure to advance the statutory mission of the Oversight Board.” The federal judge overseeing the dismissal case, however, held those ex-post communications were “fundamentally defective.”
Media reports cited complaints that the board’s outlays on consultants and legal teams were high (link requires paid subscription). Unnamed White House officials were quoted as endorsing criticisms of the board’s efforts to cut debts of the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority through the PROMESA Title III process. White House officials were also quoted as claiming that the board “has been run inefficiently and ineffectively by its governing members for far too long and it’s time to restore common sense leadership.”
Andrew Biggs and former Oversight Board Chair David Skeel defended the work of the Oversight Board and warned that the dismissals could have severe economic consequences for Puerto Rico.
What Actions Can the Oversight Board Take?
Provisions of PROMESA and bylaws established by the Oversight Board circumscribe what actions the board may take.
PROMESA itself requires no quorum for convening meetings of the Oversight Board and conducting its basic business. PROMESA (48 U.S.C. §2121(h)) does require a minimum number of votes for some of the board’s core functions.
For components of Puerto Rico’s public sector that the Oversight Board designates as “covered instrumentalities,” the board approves fiscal plans (48 U.S.C. §2141) and budgets (48 U.S.C. §2142) submitted by the governor of Puerto Rico. The Oversight Board can demand changes to those submissions, and if a revised submission does not meet PROMESA requirements, the board can develop and submit its own fiscal plan or budget for a given public-sector component. In addition, if the governor and legislature pass a law that the Oversight Board finds incompatible with a fiscal plan or PROMESA’s requirements, the board can act to prevent the enforcement or application of the law (48 U.S.C. §2144).
PROMESA requires a majority vote of the Oversight Board’s full appointed membership to approve a fiscal plan or a budget or to prevent application of a law. The board may also conduct business in executive session upon a majority vote of the Oversight Board’s full voting membership. Entering one of Puerto Rico’s public entities into the Title III debt restructuring process requires votes of at least five board members. Title VI does not appear to have similar voting requirements as those in Title III.
The Oversight Board’s bylaws, however, require a quorum to conduct the business of the board and for all other purposes. With some exceptions, actions of the Oversight Board require an affirmative vote of no fewer than four members. Appointment or removal of the board’s executive director or the general counsel requires a vote of the board chair and four other members.
If the board members number five or fewer, actions require a majority of appointed members. Appointment of an executive director or a general counsel, however, requires votes of the chair and at least three other members. Removal of the board’s executive director or the general counsel would presumably still require consent of the chair and three other members.
Amending or repealing the board’s bylaws also requires a vote of at least four members. The bylaws were last amended on April 19, 2024.
PREPA Debt Restructuring
The PROMESA Title III case for the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA) remains the last major debt restructuring process. In December 2022, the Oversight Board proposed a settlement via a plan of adjustment, which was followed by several revisions. The Board had estimated its recent offers would provide $2.6 billion to creditors. Bondholders, however, challenged the board’s assessment of terms of the underlying bond agreement. In November 2024, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in a revised decision largely sided with creditors’ claims. The district court handling the case has repeatedly urged the board and creditors to continue negotiations.
In July 2025, a coalition claiming to hold about 60% of PREPA bonds argued that electric rates should be set high enough to pay the utility’s indebtedness, which they estimate to total $12 billion.
On August 8, 2025, the federal district court handling PROMESA Title III cases suspended deadlines and ordered the Oversight Board to report on the “status of its membership and what effect, if any, the recent events will have on its participation in matters pending before the Court” by August 25, 2025. The main PREPA bondholder coalition replied that it and the apparently sole remaining Oversight Board member preferred to stay Title III proceedings until new board members were appointed.
The Oversight Board had also engaged in contentious negotiations with New Fortress Energy (NFE). The board held up a new long-term contract for natural gas after raising concerns that it could undermine “market competition and limit[] flexibility.” In mid-September 2025, the island government signed a $4 billion gas supply contract with NFE, which the Oversight Board approved subject to certain conditions. The NFE subsidiary Genera has been taking over operations of Puerto Rico’s electric generation plants.

api_metadata.summary:
On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran. The same day, President Donald Trump listed among the operation’s objectives preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, destroying Iran’s missiles, and “[razing] their missile industry to the ground.” Some Members of Congress have questioned the U.S. military operations in Iran given President Trump’s previous assertion that, as a result of the June 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes, “Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.” Other Members have supported the President’s action, citing Iran’s post-2025 efforts to reconstitute its nuclear program and its ballistic missile capabilities. Reports on the status of Iran’s missile and drone programs vary as of October 2026 amid continued, albeit reduced, military confrontation between the United States and Iran.
Iran’s Ballistic Missile and Drone Programs 
Iran has developed short- and medium-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and space-launch vehicles. Iran has also mass-produced various long-range one-way attack drones, such as the Shahed-136, and has provided drones to Russia for use in its war in Ukraine. After Israeli strikes on Iranian missile sites in 2024 and 2025, Iran “focused on rebuilding damaged infrastructure and pursuing Russia- and China-origin systems and materials to replace equipment,” according to an April 2026 U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessment.
Beginning on February 28, 2026, U.S. and Israeli aircraft targeted bases and equipment associated with Iran’s ballistic missile program, including missiles Iran may have stored in underground facilities. The White House stated on April 8, after the United States and Iran agreed to a temporary ceasefire, that the operation involved strikes on “more than 450 ballistic missile targets” and “approximately 800 attack drone targets,” and that “Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capacity has been razed.” Since April, the United States has continued to target Iranian missile and drone facilities, and Iranian ballistic missiles and drones have struck U.S. and partner military and civil sites, as well as vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
DIA assessed in April 2026 that Iran “retains thousands of missiles and one-way attack UAVs that can threaten U.S. and partner forces throughout the region, despite degradations to its capabilities from both attrition and expenditure.” News articles in July, August, and September, citing satellite imagery and U.S. and Israeli military and intelligence officials, stated that Iran may have begun rebuilding military infrastructure, restoring access to missile bases, and resuming missile production using stockpiled components. An Iranian official reportedly asserted in August that Iran has sufficient “stockpiles in our underground missile and drone cities” to enable continued production. Some reports have highlighted the damage to Iranian production facilities and the difficulties Iran may face in reconstituting its missile development and production capability.
Iran’s Nuclear Program
Iran for decades has maintained a uranium enrichment program. Uranium enrichment can produce both low-enriched uranium, which can be used in nuclear power reactors, and highly enriched uranium, which is one of the two types of fissile material used in nuclear weapons. Tehran asserts its enrichment program is only meant to produce fuel for peaceful nuclear applications.
Whether the U.S.-Israeli strikes since February 28 have affected Iran’s nuclear facilities is unclear. On March 4, based on analysis of satellite imagery, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported “no damage to facilities containing nuclear material in Iran,” but some damage “at entrances” to the Natanz enrichment facility. The agency subsequently reported that analysis of such imagery revealed “damage to additional non-nuclear-related buildings” near this facility. The IAEA, which implements safeguards on Iran’s nuclear facilities because the government is a state party to the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, withdrew inspectors from Iran in June 2025 after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. In November 2025, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran was not enriching uranium.
The IAEA has not been able to inspect the attacked Iranian nuclear facilities since the June 2025 strikes. U.S. government reports have provided differing assessments of the June 2025 strikes’ impacts. According to the 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy, the strikes “significantly degraded” Iran’s nuclear program, while the 2026 National Defense Strategy stated the strikes “obliterated” the program. 
The U.S. intelligence community has for years assessed that Iran could have the capability to produce nuclear weapons at some point, but also that Tehran halted its nuclear weapons program in late 2003 and had not mastered all of the necessary technologies for building such weapons. U.S. intelligence also assessed, through 2025, that Tehran had not reauthorized the development of nuclear weapons. Prior to the 2026 airstrikes, Iran “was intending to try to recover from the devastation of its nuclear infrastructure,” the 2026 Annual Threat Assessment (ATA) of the U.S. Intelligence Community states. On March 2, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi stated the agency had no evidence of “a structured [Iranian] program to manufacture nuclear weapons.” 
Legislative Activity
The House Armed Services Committee (HASC), in a report accompanying the HASC-reported version of a National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H.R. 8800; H.Rept. 119-698), directed the Secretary of Defense (who is using “Secretary of War” as a “secondary title” under Executive Order 14347, dated September 5, 2025) to submit to the committee a report by February 1, 2027, on the “impact of United States military operations ... on Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities.”
Considerations for Congress
Congress may consider assessing the status and scope of existing reporting requirements on Iran, including of Section 1245 of P.L. 111-84 (10 U.S.C. §113 note), which directed the Secretary of Defense to submit to Congress an “annual report on military power of Iran” by January 30 of each year. Congress has modified this requirement, including by directing the Secretary to provide additional information about Iran’s nuclear and drone programs (P.L. 119-60, §1222). Congress may consult that report to determine whether or not it should include additional information. Congress may consider directing the Pentagon to publish a public version of the report. Members could ask questions concerning the above topics during threat assessment hearings.

api_metadata.summary:
Since the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28, 2026, some Members of Congress have raised concerns about and sought information from the Department of Defense on the stockpiles and availability of munitions (e.g., ammunition, bombs, missiles, torpedoes, anti-aircraft weapons, and missile interceptors). (DOD is “using a secondary Department of War designation,” under Executive Order 14347 dated September 5, 2025.) Following the Trump Administration’s request for FY2026 supplemental funding, including $67.1 billion for military operations against Iran and other DOD activities, the House adopted a concurrent resolution (H.Con.Res. 113) that would allow for accelerated consideration of reconciliation legislation to provide $60 billion in mandatory defense funding beginning FY2027, potentially to include funding for munitions. 
In September 2026, President Donald Trump said, “we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using,” and DOD officials have said sufficient munitions are available. The DOD Office of Inspector General, citing the DOD Office of the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment, stated that “the munitions expenditure in [Operation Epic Fury] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” and that the “defense industrial base requires significant lead time’ to expand production capacities.” 
U.S. Capabilities Expended in Operations Against Iran
DOD has not made public the precise numbers of specific types of munitions expended in the conflict. The House and Senate Committees on Armed Services have reportedly received classified briefings with Administration officials on the conduct of operations. In congressional testimony on May 14, Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), stated that the U.S. military conducted more than “13,500 strikes” in the initial 38 days of “major combat operations.” The United States and regional partners “intercepted over 6,000 one-way attack drones and more than 1,500 ballistic missiles,” according to Admiral Cooper. 
An April 2026 assessment by a U.S. think tank estimated that the United States had expended substantial quantities of selected, high-cost munitions in the conflict, including Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Patriot interceptors, Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, and Tomahawk missiles. An August 2026 news article, citing U.S. officials, reported the U.S. military had expended approximately 1,700 Patriot, 200 THAAD, and 150 Standard Missile interceptors. In September 2026, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), comparing public reporting on U.S. missile defense interceptor munition purchases with reported conflict usage, estimated that the United States had “probably used between one-half and two-thirds” of its inventory of certain missile interceptors.
Cost of Expended Munitions
On June 24, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget submitted to Congress a supplemental funding request for defense and other Administration priorities that included a $21 billion request for “munitions.” Subsequently, DOD presented varying estimates of the cost of replacing munitions expended since February 2026. For example, DOD has also estimated the cost of replacing expended munitions at $27.7 billion, according to CBO. In September, CBO, citing reporting from publicly available sources on the quantities of munitions expended, estimated the cost to replace munitions expended through August 1, 2026, was $21.7 billion, including “$7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions.” CBO estimated that it “would probably take at least five years” to replace certain interceptors even at an increased rate of production. 
Congressional Action on FY2026 Supplemental Request
On July 22, the House adopted a concurrent budget resolution (H.Con.Res. 113) that included reconciliation instructions to the House Armed Services Committee to “submit changes in laws within its jurisdiction that increase the deficit” by no more than $60 billion for the period FY2027-FY2036. The resolution did not specify the amount to be allocated to munitions. In a statement, Representative Jodey Arrington, chair of the House Budget Committee, stated that the resolution would provide the “bombs, bullets, and battlefield readiness ... to finish the fight.” On July 23, the resolution was received in the Senate. As of this product’s publication date, the Senate has not considered the measure. 
Potential Considerations for Congress
Appropriations for Munitions. In FY2025 and FY2026, Congress took steps to increase munitions stockpiles and production by authorizing and appropriating funds, among other actions. Congress may consider whether or not to provide additional funds for munitions used in the Middle East. Congress may also consider whether or not to increase funding for munitions in FY2027 appropriations and subsequent years. 
Munitions Inventories. Congress is considering legislation that would require reporting on the financial cost of operations against Iran (H.R. 8800, §1089E), as well as on the status of U.S. munitions stockpiles and inventory requirements (H.R. 8800, §321; S. 4784, §872). Congress may also consider conducting oversight of related issues, such as the amount of time required to replenish munitions stocks, as well as options for low-cost alternatives to existing missile interceptors and weapons for countering drone threats.
Missile Defense Integration and Foreign Military Sales (FMS). The United States has sought to integrate missile defense efforts with allies and partners in part through sales of U.S. equipment. Finite U.S. industrial base capacity introduces trade-offs between filling FMS orders and replenishing U.S. stockpiles. FMS delivery delays may result in cancellations, potentially affecting U.S. and partner interoperability and integration. Congress is considering legislation that would require the integration of FMS demand into industrial base planning (H.R. 8800, §1817). Congress may also consider how the executive branch develops and updates prioritization criteria for FMS and whether coproduction efforts could augment U.S. capacity.
Tactical and Strategic Vulnerabilities. Congress may consider the potential vulnerabilities associated with shortages of certain munitions and reported damage to associated defense systems. In the near term, potential vulnerabilities may include a narrowing of options for sustaining operations in Iran and sustaining U.S. allies. In the medium term, Congress may assess how depleted stockpiles may affect the U.S. ability to “erect a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain” in the Indo-Pacific, as described in the 2026 National Defense Strategy.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire temporary foreign workers for specialty occupation positions (i.e., positions that require specialized knowledge and a college degree). To date in 2026 the Trump Administration has announced several policy changes aimed at addressing perceived abuses of the program, such as replacing U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign workers. These executive actions come on the heels of policy changes announced in 2025.
Increased Costs for Employers
In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) implemented a weighted (instead of random) selection process for the H-1B lottery to “favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid” workers. The first affected lottery was for H-1B employment starting in October 2026.
In March 2026, the Department of Labor (DOL) published a proposed rule to increase H-1B prevailing wage requirements. DOL asserted that under the current regulation, “employers were permitted to hire alien workers at wage levels below those that similarly employed U.S. workers were paid, resulting in adverse effects to the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers.” H-1B prevailing wage requirements differ by skill level (See Table 1), specialty occupation, and Metropolitan Statistical Area.

Source: CRS Presentation of 91 Federal Register 15454.
DOL estimated these proposed wage requirements would increase H-1B employer costs by approximately $1.46 billion in the first year.
In August 2026, DHS issued a proposed rule to establish a new $103,265 fee to “generate dedicated revenue to support the costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The new fee would apply to each cap-subject petition submitted by employers for H-1B workers. This is separate from the $100,000 fee the Administration imposed in September 2025 on U.S. employers petitioning for new H-1B workers from abroad (which was in effect for most of the past year but is currently temporarily blocked due to ongoing litigation).
In August 2026, DHS issued a final rule that applies an existing $4,000 “9-11 Biometric Fee” to petitions filed by certain employers on behalf of H-1B or L-1 workers (within-company transfers to the United States) who are extending their status. Before this rule, DHS had interpreted the 9-11 Biometric Fee passed by Congress in 2015 to apply only to petitions for new workers or those changing employers. Employers subject to this fee—before and after the change—are those with more than 50 employees in the United States, of whom more than 50 percent are in H-1B or L-1 status. The 9-11 Biometric Fee is scheduled to sunset on September 30, 2027. 
Increased Scrutiny of Employers
In July 2026, the DOL Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation and intensified enforcement efforts “to combat fraud and human trafficking” in the H-1B program, focusing on fraudulent applications and coercive wage-kickbacks. This initiative includes a nationwide awareness program encouraging workers to report concerns to DOL. It builds on the 2025 launch of “Project Firewall,” an initiative to strengthen labor enforcement of the H-1B program by “prioritizing investigations where there are signs of displacements, inadequate recruitment of U.S. workers, or other abuses.” Data on DOL H-1B compliance enforcement actions in FY2026 are not yet available.
In September 2026, President Trump issued an executive order, requiring more coordination between agencies to “ensure the compliance ... with statutory requirements” and requires them to “take into account in any labor condition application, petition, visa, and entry of aliens entering or attempting to enter the United States as H-1B nonimmigrants ... whether the employer sponsor directly or indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year or plans future layoffs.” Current law does not bar employers with recent layoffs of U.S. workers from employing H-1B workers. DHS is also considering “revising eligibility for cap exemptions, providing greater scrutiny for employers that have violated program requirements, and increasing oversight over third party placements.” 
In October 2026, DHS proposed removing a policy of deferring to prior approvals when employers petition to extend H-1B workers’ employment. Removing “prior deference” would increase scrutiny of extension requests when the circumstances of H-1B employment are unchanged.
Restrictions for Workers
In September 2026, DHS proposed eliminating a grace period (implemented in 2017), which allows H-1B and certain other temporary workers to remain in the United States for up to 60 days after their employment ends. In October, DHS eliminated automatic extensions of work authorization for spouses of H-1B workers and is considering removing their eligibility for work authorization altogether. 
Some employers sponsor their H-1B workers for permanent labor certification (known as PERM). If approved, these workers may become LPRs, which allows them to more easily change employers (and to eventually become U.S. citizens). The administration has initiated rulemaking “improving the minimum standards for recruiting qualified U.S. workers, strengthening safeguards for U.S. workers impacted by layoffs, and enhancing employer compliance with program requirements related to non-discriminatory recruitment and hiring practices.” Such changes could result in fewer H-1B workers being approved for PERM. 
Impacts Thus Far
There are indications that employers are filing fewer petitions for H-1B workers coming from abroad. DHS data show reduced petition filings from both cap-subject and cap-exempt employers following the implementation of the $100,000 fee in 2025. For example, during the first eight months that the fee was in effect, the number of initial H-1B petitions that DHS received for consular processing from cap-exempt employers dropped 91% from the same period the year before. Similarly, cap-subject companies that typically had high numbers of H-1B employees coming from abroad submitted significantly fewer entries to the FY2027 H-1B lottery. Among the highest lottery entrants in FY2026 were Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata, which submitted 100%, 91%, and 95% fewer registrations in FY2027, respectively.

On October 1, 2026, the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) published for comment revised policy guidance for the Capital Investment Grants Program (CIG). In the Federal Register notice, FTA stated “the proposed revisions are intended to streamline the CIG process, improve accountability of CIG project sponsors, and improve overall readability of the policy guidance.” Among other things, FTA proposes a new formal methodology for calculating the federal share of a proposed project’s cost from a CIG grant. This proposed methodology includes greater CIG funding shares for projects in places with higher than average birth rates and marriage rates, in line with the Department of Transportation’s (DOT’s) “family friendly” policy.
CIG provides funding to support the construction of fixed-guideway transit systems (e.g., light rail), including new systems and additions to existing systems. A CIG project is categorized as a “New Starts” project, unless as a “Small Starts” project it costs less than $400 million and CIG program funding is less than $150 million. “Core Capacity” projects are investments in existing fixed-guideway systems that increase capacity of a corridor by 10% that is at or will be at capacity in 10 years (49 U.S.C. §5309(a)).
To evaluate proposed CIG projects, FTA computes ratings of statutory project justification and local financial commitment criteria on a 5-point scale (high, medium-high, medium, medium-low, low). The project justification criteria are mobility improvements, environmental benefits, congestion relief, economic development effects, land use (or capacity needs of the corridor for Core Capacity projects), and cost effectiveness. Cost effectiveness, for example, is measured by estimated capital and operating and maintenance costs per trip.
Federal law limits the maximum federal share of a project’s cost from the CIG program funds to 60% for New Starts projects and 80% for Small Starts and Core Capacity projects (49 U.S.C. §5309(l)). Many projects have received a commitment from FTA for a CIG share below the maximum. 
FTA’s October 2026 proposal is for a “formal methodology [that] would provide a uniform and consistent approach for FTA to consider project merits, such as cost-effectiveness and transit ridership, when determining the CIG percentage share and corresponding CIG funding amount for a New Starts or Core Capacity project.” Accordingly, projects with an overall medium or higher rating would start with a 40% CIG share of project costs. This share would then be adjusted on the basis of the ratings of the project justification criteria up to the maximum allowed by law (Table 1). FTA states that it “believes these adjustment factors are appropriate because they clearly put the emphasis on cost-effectiveness and ridership, which will allow FTA to provide a higher CIG percentage share to projects that are cost-effective and projected to have high transit ridership, and will ensure Federal taxpayer funds are supporting worthy investments.”

Source: Federal Transit Administration, “Notice of Availability of Proposed Policy Guidance for the Capital Investment Grants Program,” 91 Federal Register 62586-62595, October 1, 2026.
Note: *New Starts only; **Core Capacity only.
FTA’s proposed CIG policy would also increase the CIG funding share for relatively high birth rates and marriage rates within the project corridor, defined as a one-mile buffer around the project corridor using census tract data from the Census Bureau. The increase would be an additional five percentage points each if the average birth or marriage rate in the project corridor is more than 1% above the national average, three points if the birth or marriage rate is equal to the national average or up to 1% percent higher than the national average, and one point if the average birth or marriage rate is within 1% below the national average. 
According to FTA, these proposed adjustments are consistent with DOT Order 2100.7, “Ensuring Reliance Upon Sound Economic Analysis in Department of Transportation Policies, Programs, and Activities,” issued on March 10, 2025, by the Secretary of Transportation. The order states DOT should “give preference to communities with marriage and birth rates higher than the national average (including in administering the Federal Transit Administration’s Capital Investment Grant program).”
Some question whether this proposed addition to the funding share calculation, as FTA states in the Federal Register notice, would “ensure Federal taxpayer funds are supporting worthy investments.” The birth rate and marriage rate adjustments may offset poorer scores on other metrics, possibly leading to less effective projects. For example, together high birth rate and marriage rate adjustments can be worth as much as a medium-low cost effectiveness score.
In terms of ridership, fixed-guideway transit modes are most effective in high density urban corridors. Critics of the FTA proposal point to research on the geography of birth rates and marriage rates indicating that places with relatively high rates tend to be located farther away from urban centers than places with relatively low rates. Households in high birth and high marriage rate areas tend to be higher income, more likely to own a car and drive alone to work, and less likely to walk, bike, or take public transit to work. Residents of places with high marriage and high birth rates are more likely to be White and less likely to be Black or Hispanic. 
Adjusting the federal CIG funding share on the basis of marriage and birth rates may incentivize more commuter rail projects, which are designed to provide longer distance trips to outlying places with lower density uses. In a study of commuter rail agencies, the Government Accountability Office found that commuter rail can provide economic and mobility benefits for less urbanized communities but that there are “considerable infrastructure and operational costs making commuter rail more expensive to provide compared to some other transit modes.”

This Insight provides information and analysis related to U.S. circuit and district court nominations confirmed during lame duck sessions held by the Senate during the postwar period (i.e., since 1946). For the purpose of this Insight, a lame duck session is defined as any portion of a Congress’s regular session that occurs after the general election in November but before the end of its constitutional term on January 3 of the next calendar year.
The primary purpose of lame duck sessions during this period was to complete congressional action on legislation, including program authorizations and appropriations legislation (see CRS Report R45154 for additional information about lame duck sessions of Congress).
Lame duck sessions held by the Senate have also been used to consider a President’s judicial nominations. Of the 21 lame duck sessions held by the Senate during the postwar period, at least one U.S. circuit or district court nomination was confirmed in 16 (76%) of the sessions. These 16 lame duck sessions are reported in Figure 1. 
During this same period, the Senate did not confirm any circuit or district court nominations during lame duck sessions held in 1948 (80th Congress), 1994 (103rd Congress), 2000 (106th Congress), 2008 (110th Congress), or 2016 (114th Congress). These sessions are not included in Figure 1.
Number Confirmed
As shown by Figure 1, the Senate confirmed a total of 22 circuit court nominations and 163 district court nominations during 16 lame duck sessions held from 1950 to 2024. The greatest number of circuit court nominations confirmed during a lame duck session was five, which occurred in 2010 at the end of the 111th Congress. The greatest number of district court nominations confirmed during a lame duck session was 27, which occurred in 2014 at the end of the 113th Congress.
At least half of the circuit and district court nominations confirmed during lame duck sessions since 1948 were confirmed during the three most recent past presidencies. Overall, 11 (50%) of the 22 circuit court nominations confirmed during lame duck sessions since 1948 were confirmed during seven of the eight lame duck sessions held since 2010, as were 97 (60%) of the 163 district court nominations.
The relatively high number of circuit and district court nominations confirmed during recent lame duck sessions coincides, in part, with the reinterpretation of Senate Rule XXII during the 113th Congress to allow cloture to be invoked on most nominations by a majority of Senators voting (a quorum being present), instead of by three-fifths of the Senate.
Figure 1. Lame Duck Sessions of Congress During Which U.S. Circuit or District Court Nominations Were Confirmed
(1950-2024)
/
Source: Congressional Research Service.
Notes: The Senate did not confirm any circuit or district court nominations during lame duck sessions held in 1948, 1994, 2000, 2008, or 2016. These sessions are not listed in Figure 1.
Type of Preceding Election
During this period, it was more common for circuit and district court nominations to be confirmed during lame duck sessions that followed midterm elections than presidential elections. Of the 22 circuit court nominations confirmed, 19 (86%) were confirmed during a lame duck session that followed a midterm election, while 3 (14%) were confirmed during a session that followed a presidential election. These three nominees were Stephen G. Breyer (confirmed to the First Circuit in 1980), Thomas L. Kirsch II (confirmed to the Seventh Circuit in 2020), and Embry J. Kidd (confirmed to the Eleventh Circuit in 2024).
Of the 163 district court nominations confirmed, 114 (70%) were confirmed during a lame duck session that followed a midterm election, while 49 (30%) were confirmed during a session that followed a presidential election. Of the latter group of 49 nominees, 46 (94%) were confirmed during lame duck sessions that followed the 2012, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections.
When Nominations Were Submitted
During this period, it was more common for circuit and district court nominations confirmed during lame duck sessions to have been formally submitted by a President before an election, than after it.
Of the 22 circuit court nominations confirmed, 15 (68%) were formally nominated before an election and 7 (32%) were nominated after the election. For the 15 nominations submitted prior to an election, the average number of days a nomination was first submitted prior to an election date was 245 days (8.1 months).
Of the 163 district court nominations confirmed, 127 (78%) were formally nominated before an election and 36 (22%) were nominated after the election. For the 127 nominations submitted prior to an election, the average number of days a nomination was first submitted prior to an election was 153 days (5.0 months).
When Nominations Were Confirmed
Circuit and district court nominations confirmed during lame duck sessions were confirmed, on average, 36 and 31 days, respectively, after election dates during this period. There have been instances, however, of shorter lengths of time from an election date to a nomination being confirmed. For example, during the lame duck session for the 107th Congress, there were 17 district court nominations confirmed by voice vote on November 14, 2002—nine days following the 2002 election.
Changes in Majority Party Control
The Senate has confirmed circuit and district court nominations during lame duck sessions which followed elections that led to a change in majority party control of the Senate in the next Congress. In the period covered by Figure 1, this occurred for the first time in 1954. As of this writing, it most recently occurred in 2024 during the lame duck session for the 118th Congress, when the Senate confirmed one circuit court nomination and 21 district court nominations.
Other Types of Judgeships
While not included within the scope of this Insight, the Senate has also confirmed judges to other types of federal courts during lame duck sessions held since 1946—including the U.S. Court of International Trade, the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, and the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. 
Since the Twentieth Amendment was ratified in 1933, which shortened the period of time from when a general election occurred to when Members-elect began their constitutional terms in office, there has not been, as of this writing, a Supreme Court Justice confirmed during a lame duck session of Congress. The most recent nominee confirmed during a lame duck session prior to the ratification of the Twentieth Amendment was Harlan Fiske Stone—who was confirmed on February 5, 1925, during the second session of the 68th Congress, which followed the election on November 4, 1924.
