api_metadata.summary:
In 1999, the Supreme Court decided the landmark disability discrimination case Olmstead v. L.C. ex rel. Zimring, which established that “unjustified institutional isolation of persons with disabilities is a form of discrimination.” Olmstead applied Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA Title II), which prohibits disability discrimination by state and local governments. Title II is often interpreted consistently with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 504), which prohibits disability discrimination by recipients of federal funding and federal agencies. When Olmstead was decided, long-standing Title II and Section 504 regulations from the Department of Justice (DOJ) required covered entities to serve people with disabilities “in the most integrated setting appropriate to the[ir] needs.” Section 504 regulations from other agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), echoed this “integration mandate.” 
On June 18, 2026, the DOJ Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published an opinion (OLC Opinion) narrowing DOJ’s interpretation of Olmstead. OLC determined that Olmstead, Section 504, and Title II do not “impose[] an integration mandate.” Rather than requiring services in integrated settings, OLC interpreted Olmstead, Title II, and Section 504 to prohibit only the irrational institutionalization of people with disabilities. Subsequently, DOJ has withdrawn from or changed its position in several Olmstead matters on grounds related to the OLC Opinion and for other cited reasons. These matters include a case challenging HHS’s regulations implementing the integration mandate. As a result of DOJ’s change in position, the HHS integration regulations have been vacated. 
This Legal Sidebar reviews the background of the integration mandate and the Olmstead decision. It discusses OLC’s new interpretation of Olmstead and certain recent DOJ activities related to Olmstead enforcement. It concludes with some potential implications of these developments.
Section 504, Title II, and the Integration Mandate
Section 504 prohibits disability discrimination by federal funding recipients and federal agencies, and Title II prohibits disability discrimination by state and local governments. The integration mandate has been part of Section 504’s interpretation since its original regulations were promulgated, and it was adopted into Title II’s regulations after the ADA’s passage as well. Relevant to the Supreme Court’s holding in Olmstead, both statutes have also consistently been interpreted to require covered entities to make reasonable modifications to accommodate people with disabilities.
Because Section 504 attaches conditions to federal funding, each federal agency promulgates Section 504 regulations governing its grantees. Responsibility for coordinating federal Section 504 enforcement originally rested with the former Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) and was later shifted to DOJ. HEW promulgated regulations coordinating executive agency implementation of Section 504 in 1978, and DOJ adopted those regulations in full in 1981. They have not been substantively amended since. The Section 504 coordination regulations require recipients of federal funding to, among other things, “administer programs and activities in the most integrated setting appropriate to the needs of qualified handicapped persons.” At the time of promulgation, HEW described this requirement as “intrinsic to section 504.” 
When Congress passed the ADA in 1990, it included findings that “historically, society has tended to isolate and segregate individuals with disabilities” and described “such forms of discrimination” as “a serious and pervasive social problem.” It directed DOJ to issue Title II regulations “consistent with” the 1978 HEW Section 504 coordination regulations. Since 1991, DOJ’s Title II regulations have therefore paralleled the Section 504 coordination regulations, requiring state and local governments to “administer services, programs, and activities in the most integrated setting appropriate to the needs of qualified individuals with disabilities.” Under the regulations, the “most integrated setting” is the “setting that enables individuals with disabilities to interact with nondisabled persons to the fullest extent possible.” In 1991, DOJ stated: “Integration is fundamental to the purposes of the [ADA].”
In 2011, DOJ published guidance on the integration mandate. That guidance affirmed DOJ’s perspective at the time that the ADA required covered entities to “provide individuals with disabilities opportunities to live, work, and receive services in the greater community” and that people “at serious risk of institutionalization or segregation” could bring ADA claims. The guidance rejected the notion that costs to state programs could, on their own, justify serving people with disabilities in more segregated settings.
The Supreme Court and federal agencies have also interpreted Section 504 and Title II to require covered entities to make reasonable modifications to allow people with disabilities to access their programs and services. In Alexander v. Choate, a Section 504 case, the Court held that “while a grantee need not be required to make fundamental’ or substantial’ modifications to accommodate the handicapped, it may be required to make reasonable’ ones.” Both Title II’s statutory text and its regulations require reasonable modifications. Like Section 504, Title II does not require covered entities to make changes that “would fundamentally alter the nature of the service, program, or activity.”
Olmstead v. L.C. ex rel. Zimring
In Olmstead, two women with intellectual disabilities and serious mental illnesses sued Georgia health officials for allegedly keeping them institutionalized for years after their physicians agreed that they could be served in community-based programs. The plaintiffs argued that Georgia violated the Title II integration mandate by failing to place them in such programs. Georgia countered that the plaintiffs had not shown disability discrimination because they could not identify a group of similarly situated nondisabled people who were treated better. Georgia contended that it was keeping plaintiffs out of community-based services not because of their disabilities but because of costs, and requiring the state to prioritize particular services for these two individuals would fundamentally alter its health program by forcing it to divert funds from serving other people with medical needs.
Majority Opinion
A splintered Supreme Court largely sided with the plaintiffs. In the majority opinion authored by Justice Ginsburg, the Court held that “unjustified institutional isolation of persons with disabilities is a form of discrimination” prohibited by Title II. The Court relied both on Congress’s findings in the ADA, which “explicitly identified unjustified segregation’ of persons with disabilities as a for[m] of discrimination,’” and DOJ’s Title II regulations requiring integrated services. The Court reasoned that unjustified institutionalization was a form of discrimination for at least two reasons: First, it “perpetuates” stereotypes that people with disabilities “are incapable or unworthy of participating in community life.” Second, it results in disparate treatment of people with disabilities because it requires them to “relinquish participation in community life they could enjoy given reasonable accommodations, while persons without mental disabilities can receive the medical services they need without similar sacrifice.”
A majority of the Court also agreed that a state could defer to the “reasonable assessments of its own professionals” as to appropriate medical placements and that a state did not need to put unwilling patients in community-based services. In other words, to be eligible to transfer to a more integrated setting, a person with a disability would need to consent and obtain a doctor’s approval.
How much Olmstead’s holding depended on DOJ’s Title II regulations is not clear. One could read the opinion as an interpretation of DOJ’s regulations. The Court characterized the dispute between the parties, at least in part, as one over “the proper construction and enforcement of the regulations.” The Court expressly declined to consider whether the regulations validly construed Title II, and it therefore may have based its conclusion on the assumption that they did. On the other hand, the Court also characterized the case as “concern[ing] the proper construction” of Title II itself, not just the regulations, and it appeared to treat the regulations as one of several sources of support for its holding. It declined to decide whether it should defer to DOJ’s regulations under the then-prevailing Chevron doctrine, holding only that DOJ’s “views warrant respect.” The Court also looked to congressional findings and its own reasoning about what discrimination means, in addition to its references to the Title II regulations.
Plurality Opinion
As discussed above, a majority of the Court in Olmstead agreed that unjustified institutionalization can be disability discrimination and that states need not provide community-based services against a doctor’s advice or a patient’s wishes. The Court did not reach a majority to further explain when public entities must provide community-based services. A four-member plurality viewed the matter as a question of what reasonable modifications states would need to make to provide community-based care to participants in state medical programs. The plurality sought to balance the needs of people in institutions seeking more integrated settings with “the responsibility the State has undertaken for the care and treatment of a large and diverse population of persons with mental disabilities.” In addition to a doctor’s approval and patient’s consent, the plurality thought that a state would have to provide community-based services when “the placement can be reasonably accommodated, taking into account the resources available to the State and the needs of others with mental disabilities.” Generally, the plurality thought that a state could meet its obligations by showing that it had a “working plan for placing qualified persons with mental disabilities in less restrictive settings, and a waiting list that moved at a reasonable pace not controlled by the State’s endeavors to keep its institutions fully populated.”
Justice Kennedy’s Concurrence
Justice Kennedy concurred in the judgment. While he did not join the majority opinion, he agreed that institutionalization could constitute disability discrimination. Justice Kennedy proposed, however, that plaintiffs pleading a Title II claim based on unjustified institutionalization would have to show that the state served another group of people with “medical problems of comparable seriousness” in the community but denied community-based services to the plaintiffs because of their disabilities. Justice Kennedy emphasized his concerns that courts respect doctors’ treatment recommendations, that federal courts not overly intrude into state health policy decisions (including by managing trade-offs between competing interests), and that people with disabilities not be forced out of institutions without proper treatment or placements available in the community.
Dissent
Justice Thomas, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Scalia, dissented. The dissent would have found discrimination only if the state treated a person in a protected group—in this case, people with disabilities—differently than people outside that group. Because the plaintiffs in Olmstead sought services given only to people with disabilities, in the dissent’s view they could not identify anyone outside of their protected class who was treated better. The dissent saw the plaintiff’s claim as one for a certain “standard of care,” rather than nondiscriminatory treatment. The dissent also echoed Justice Kennedy’s concerns about the “federalism costs” of “directing States how to make decisions about their delivery of public services” and about undue court interference in state decisions about the allocation of “limited resources.”
DOJ’s Reinterpretation of Olmstead
The 2026 OLC Opinion significantly changes DOJ’s interpretation of Olmstead, Section 504, and Title II. As described above, since 1981, DOJ has consistently interpreted Section 504 and Title II to require covered entities to maximize integration when serving people with disabilities. The OLC Opinion concludes that federal agencies “incorrectly interpret [the laws] to impose an integration mandate.” OLC acknowledges that most circuit courts treat the Olmstead plurality’s framework “as binding.” OLC, however, emphasizes what it describes as the majority’s “narrow” holding: that Title II prohibits only “unjustified institutional isolation.” Further, OLC interprets the majority to say “remarkably little” about when institutionalization is “unjustified.” OLC interprets Section 504, Title II, and Olmstead to prohibit institutionalization “only when there are no legitimate, nondiscriminatory factors that weigh in favor of it.” In OLC’s view, legitimate justifications for institutionalization include anything other than the “mere fact of disability” itself. OLC elaborates that this may “include concerns about the safety of the individual or the community,” such as that disabled individuals will not take “necessary medication”; “[r]esource and space constraints in community-based treatment facilities”; or any “special needs resulting from” a person’s disability.
In many ways, the OLC Opinion echoes the concerns of Justice Kennedy’s concurrence and the Olmstead dissent. OLC opines that requiring states to provide medical services in integrated settings would be constitutionally suspect for a number of reasons, including that it would “upset the usual constitutional balance of federal and state powers.” It contends that the fundamental meaning of discrimination is to treat similarly situated people differently and that institutionalization is therefore discriminatory only when a covered entity makes “arbitrary distinctions between individuals with similar medical needs.” Beyond some of the reasoning supported by the concurring and dissenting Justices in Olmstead, OLC doubts whether Congress has the constitutional authority to regulate where states provide medical services outside of attaching conditions to federal funds, and it does not think that Section 504 speaks clearly enough to the integration mandate to give recipients the necessary “clear notice” of what is required.
On July 20, 2026, DOJ published a Federal Register notice to “clarify” that certain DOJ Olmstead guidance, including the 2011 guidance, is “not enforceable” and that DOJ would not rely on it. According to the notice, DOJ intends to “revisit” whether its Olmstead guidance is “consistent with the single, best meaning’” of the ADA.
Recent DOJ Activities Related to Olmstead Enforcement
DOJ and HHS have cited the OLC Opinion and July 20, 2026, notice to explain changes in their litigating positions in ongoing Olmstead matters. In one such case, Texas v. Kennedy, HHS faced a suit from several states challenging its Section 504 regulations implementing the integration mandate. The states claimed that HHS had exceeded its statutory authority by forcing states to “redesign their entire systems of care” to provide HHS’s preferred services, rather than requiring only that states not discriminate in the services they did provide. In addition, the states claimed HHS violated Spending Clause requirements by attaching “new conditions” to federal funds that were coercive and not clearly statutorily mandated.
Citing the OLC Opinion, HHS and the plaintiffs in Texas v. Kennedy agreed to settle the case by jointly asking the court to vacate HHS’s integration-related Section 504 regulations. On September 23, 2026, the court obliged. The court’s order vacates the challenged regulations nationwide. The court observed that DOJ takes the position that courts cannot vacate rules and that any vacatur “must at least be party-specific” but stated that DOJ agreed not to “pursue [that] position . . . in this case.”
DOJ cited its July 20, 2026, notice to explain its request to the Eleventh Circuit to vacate a recent decision in DOJ’s favor in another case, United States v. Florida, which DOJ had been litigating since 2013. United States v. Florida involved claims that Florida administered its Medicaid program in ways that put children with “complex medical needs” in nursing homes or “at serious risk” of institutionalization. The suit addressed “approximately 140 Institutionalized Children” and “more than 1,800” children at risk of institutionalization. Ultimately, DOJ prevailed on a number of significant legal issues, among them that people “at risk of institutionalization” could bring claims under Title II. In March 2026, the Eleventh Circuit largely upheld an injunction requiring Florida to make changes to its Medicaid administration.
In its motion to vacate, DOJ cited the July 20, 2026, notice and asked the appellate court to withdraw its decision. It stated that DOJ had “decided to revisit’” the position that people at risk of institutionalization could pursue Title II claims and that “the United States no longer seeks or wishes to enforce liability in this case based on the at-risk theory.” It further stated that it no longer seeks to “uphold or enforce” the lower court’s injunction. In response, the Eleventh Circuit referred the case to mediation and invited “counsel representing the interests of at-risk children” to join.
In addition to changing its positions in Texas v. Kennedy and United States v. Florida, DOJ has recently withdrawn from or terminated some additional Olmstead matters. For example, on August 6, 2026, DOJ withdrew as plaintiff-intervenor and stipulated to dismissal of its claims in Steward v. Abbott. In 2025, the district court in that case held that Texas violated the ADA and Section 504 by failing to provide certain services to nursing home residents with intellectual disabilities, leaving many “languishing in nursing facilities for years when they could have been living in a community setting.” In another example, on September 14, 2026, a federal district court granted a joint motion by DOJ and North Carolina to terminate a 2012 settlement agreement related to the alleged over-institutionalization of people with serious mental illnesses.
Implications of DOJ’s Recent Approach to Olmstead and Considerations for Congress
Both Title II and Section 504 may be enforced via a private right of action, and neither private plaintiffs nor courts are bound by DOJ’s interpretation of Olmstead. Private plaintiffs may still seek to enforce an interpretation of Olmstead that requires greater access to community care, and they may seek judicial relief for people with disabilities at risk of institutionalization. 
That said, Congress envisioned that the federal government would “play[] a central role in enforcing” the ADA, and DOJ is a major player in Olmstead matters. Olmstead matters can be “highly resource- and personnel-intensive.” As in United States v. Florida, they can span years (sometimes decades), require expertise in law, health care policy and administration, medicine, and other fields, and involve dozens to thousands of plaintiffs or class members. DOJ has at times taken a “sweeping” “enforcement approach,” addressing “all of a state’s institutions” rather than individual facilities. Private litigants may lack the resources or expertise to pursue Olmstead cases at the scale at which DOJ is capable. Resource constraints aside, as commentators observe, privately litigated Olmstead matters often proceed as class actions, and class certification presents significant challenges that DOJ does not face. 
DOJ’s position has directly affected individual cases and could lead to more changes in ongoing Olmstead matters. The OLC Opinion states that DOJ “has successfully elicited consent decrees, remedial orders, or out-of-court agreements in nearly a dozen states.” As seen in the cases described above, DOJ may seek to terminate or modify other injunctions, orders, or consent decrees. DOJ’s position may enable states to exercise more flexibility in how they administer their health care programs and to allocate resources differently than they would under a more aggressive interpretation of the ADA and Section 504.
While Olmstead and the OLC Opinion focus on the integration mandate in health care settings, they each have broader implications. Olmstead’s reach stretches into other areas. DOJ has pursued Olmstead cases involving segregated employment and segregated educational services for people with disabilities, for example. Policies in these domains may be affected by the OLC Opinion. The OLC Opinion may also signal a narrower approach to Title II enforcement beyond matters involving segregation. The OLC Opinion questions Congress’s Commerce Clause authority to regulate state activity that DOJ views as noneconomic, as well as Congress’s Fourteenth Amendment authority to address disability discrimination by states except where such discrimination is irrational. One possible conclusion of this reasoning may be that Congress cannot use these constitutional authorities, which underpin Title II, to compel states to reasonably accommodate people with disabilities in all state services. Whether DOJ will extend its reasoning so far, and change its enforcement practices in other ADA cases, remains to be seen.
Olmstead is a statutory opinion. Congress can clarify its position on the integration mandate. If Congress agrees with DOJ’s approach and seeks to rein in private litigation, for example, it can amend Title II and Section 504 to align with the OLC Opinion. Congress can also consider codifying the Olmstead plurality or other approaches to a broader integration mandate. While DOJ posits certain constitutional limits on Congress’s power to require states to provide integrated services, those views have not been tested at the Supreme Court. Moreover, DOJ agrees that Congress could require integration through conditions on federal funds, so long as those conditions are clear and the law satisfies other constitutional constraints.
All Justices in Olmstead recognized that states have competing interests when serving people with disabilities and that states may lack the resources to both maintain institutions for those who need them and provide community-based services for all who could benefit from them. Resolutions in Olmstead cases may lead to both increased community-based services and decreased institutional capacity. Congress may choose to address the balance between institutional and community-based services through adjustments to its spending programs, such as Medicaid, rather than rely on civil rights law.

api_metadata.summary:
The U.S. Courts of Appeals for the thirteen “circuits” issue thousands of precedential decisions each year. Because relatively few of these decisions are ultimately reviewed by the Supreme Court, the U.S. Courts of Appeals are often the last word on consequential legal questions. The federal appellate courts sometimes reach different conclusions on the same issue of federal law, causing a “split” among the circuits that leads to the nonuniform application of federal law among similarly situated litigants.
This Legal Sidebar discusses circuit splits that emerged or widened following decisions from August 2026 on matters relevant to Congress. The Sidebar does not address every circuit split that developed or widened during this period. Selected cases typically involve judicial disagreement over the interpretation or validity of federal statutes and regulations, or constitutional issues relevant to Congress’s lawmaking and oversight functions. The Sidebar includes only cases where an appellate court’s controlling opinion recognizes a split among the circuits on a key legal issue resolved in the opinion. This Sidebar refers to each U.S. Court of Appeals by its number or descriptor (e.g., “D.C. Circuit” for “U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit”).
Some cases identified in this Sidebar, or the legal questions they address, are examined in other CRS general distribution products. Members of Congress and congressional staff may click here to subscribe to the CRS Legal Update and receive regular notifications of new products and upcoming seminars by CRS attorneys.
Arbitration: The Seventh Circuit affirmed a lower court’s denial of a defendant’s motion to compel arbitration, holding that the district court did not commit clear error in denying the motion after the lower court found that the defendant’s actions before class certification waived its right to compel arbitration. The panel decided that the Supreme Court’s 2018 decision in U.S. Bank National Association v. Village at Lakeridge, LLC abrogated earlier circuit precedent that applied a de novo standard of review to all denials of motions to compel arbitration. The panel declared that post-Lakeridge, the standard of review that applies to lower court decisions on a mixed question of law and fact depends on whether the question involves primarily legal or factual issues. Those aspects of a lower court’s decision that expound on the law and, if upheld, would have a precedential effect on future cases are reviewed de novo. However, mixed questions involving “case-specific factual considerations” are reviewed for clear error. In the panel’s view, waiver decisions are mixed questions of law and fact and thus should be reviewed for clear error, except to the extent the decision announces a new legal rule. The panel observed that it split with the First, Second, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, and Eleventh Circuits that, post-Lakeridge, have continued to uniformly apply the de novo standard to the review of denials of motions to compel arbitration, including when the basis for the denial was a party’s waiver of a right to arbitrate (Moore v. Club Exploria, LLC).
Civil Procedure: A divided Ninth Circuit panel upheld a district court’s award of attorney’s fees to the defendant in a false-advertising case brought under the Lanham Act. The Act allows awards of fees in “exceptional cases.” The panel majority held that the district court did not abuse its discretion in deciding that standard was satisfied here because the plaintiffs pursued their suit against the defendant despite repeated dismissals of similar claims they had brought in other cases. The majority also held that the defendant could recover attorney’s fees as part of “costs” under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(d), which permits the recovery of “costs” accrued when a plaintiff who voluntarily dismissed an action in any court then files an action based on the same claim against the same defendant. The majority observed that circuit courts had taken varied approaches to assess the availability of attorney’s fees under Rule 41(d). The majority described itself as aligning most closely with the Fourth and Fifth Circuits in holding that attorney’s fees can be awarded under Rule 41(d) if the statute underlying the litigation provides for the award of attorney’s fees, as was the case here. The majority acknowledged a split with published opinions by the Second and Eighth Circuits, which the majority described as holding that attorney’s fees may be awarded under Rule 41(d) at the discretion of the court, and the Sixth Circuit, which holds that attorney’s fees are never available under Rule 41(d) (ThermoLife Int'l, LLC v. BPI Sports, LLC).
Civil Procedure: The Tenth Circuit held that it lacked jurisdiction to review a post-judgment contempt order directing the appellant to stop violating an earlier injunction or show cause as to why the violation occurred. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, circuit courts have appellate jurisdiction over “final” district court decisions. The Tenth Circuit reasoned that it lacked jurisdiction to review the contempt order under § 1291 because the lower court’s order would not be final unless it made a contempt finding and imposed a sanction on a party. The panel observed that its interpretation of § 1291 conflicted with the approach taken by the Third Circuit in a few cases in which it exercised appellate jurisdiction over post-judgment enforcement orders in the absence of a contempt finding and sanction (Fischer v. XTO Energy).
Civil Procedure: In a dispute over application of the federal officer removal statute, the Eleventh Circuit held that removal of a case from state to federal court was proper when a municipality brought suit against private parties for pollutants emanating from a Superfund site designated by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Under 28 U.S.C. § 1442, a suit against a private party “acting under” a federal officer may be removed to federal court if it relates to the party’s assistance in the performance of the officer’s official duties. In this case, the federal district court had concluded that the defendant had not satisfied the criteria for removal, ordered remand of the suit to state court, and denied the defendant's request that the district court stay its remand order pending appeal. Following the district court’s remand, state court litigation against the defendant proceeded while its appeal to the Eleventh Circuit was pending. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the lower court’s decision, holding that removal to federal court was proper because the defendants’ alleged liability arose from their obligations under an EPA-mandated consent decree to remediate the site, which the EPA would otherwise have had to remediate under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act. Agreeing with the Fourth Circuit and splitting with the Ninth Circuit, the panel held that the Supreme Court's decision in Coinbase, Inc. v. Bielski, which mandates automatic stays for interlocutory appeals of arbitration denials, also applies in the federal officer removal context. Here, the panel held that Coinbase required an automatic stay of all district court proceedings, including its remand order, pending resolution of the appeal, irrespective of the subsequent state proceedings, and the lower court erred in refusing to stay its decision while that appeal was pending. The panel therefore reversed the district court’s remand of the case to state court (City of Brunswick v. Honeywell Int’l, Inc.).
Civil Procedure: A divided Ninth Circuit panel held that a federal district court erred when it blocked the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) from collecting on a money judgment against the operator of an alleged telemarketing scheme and his wife under the Federal Debt Collection Procedure Act (FDCPA). Both federal and state laws address debt collection, and while states typically provide statutes of limitations for the collection of debts in their jurisdictions, the FDCPA provides no statute of limitations for the enforcement of “debts” against the United States. Here, the lower court held that the FTC could not pursue the debt collection because it was time-barred under state law. The lower court reasoned that the FDCPA did not govern the debt collection, because the proceeds that the FTC sought were intended for disbursement to the defendants’ victims, not the United States. On appeal, the panel majority rejected this interpretation of the FDCPA (which the First Circuit had also adopted), instead holding that, because the proceeds would immediately be paid to the FTC, the judgment constituted a “debt” under the FDCPA regardless of the ultimate disbursement to private parties (FTC v. Hoskins).
Criminal Law & Procedure: The Fourth Circuit affirmed a criminal defendant’s convictions and sentence for health-care-fraud-related offenses targeting Medicare beneficiaries, including his sentencing enhancement under § 2B1.1(b)(2)(A)(ii) of the Sentencing Guidelines for committing an offense through “mass marketing.” The Guidelines define mass-marketing as a “plan, program, promotion, or campaign that is conducted through solicitation by telephone, mail, the Internet, or other means to induce a large number of persons” to, among other things, “purchase goods or services.” The defendant argued that § 2B1.1(b)(2)(A)(ii) did not apply because, although he engaged in a marketing campaign that targeted Medicare beneficiaries, those individuals suffered no loss and were not victims of his conduct. Rather, the Medicare program was the only entity that sustained a loss due to his fraudulent activity. The Fourth Circuit rejected this argument, holding that the plain text of § 2B1.1(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires only that the offender targeted a large number of persons, regardless of whether they are directly harmed by the defendant’s actions. In doing so, the Fourth Circuit split from the Second and Eighth Circuits, which read the Guidelines provision to focus on the offender’s victims. The Fourth Circuit described its decision as consistent with rulings by the Fifth and Eleventh Circuits (United States v. Joyner).
Criminal Law & Procedure: The Fourth Circuit created a circuit split over the meaning of 18 U.S.C. § 4243, which governs the revocation of conditional discharges from civil commitment for persons who were institutionalized after being found not guilty by reason of insanity. The lower court had revoked a former criminal defendant’s conditional discharge from civil commitment after he robbed a store at gunpoint, in violation of a discharge condition that prohibited him from possessing weapons. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit joined the Eleventh Circuit in deciding that the plain text of § 4243 authorized the revocation of a conditional discharge of civil commitment only when the released individual violated a discharge condition that was part of a “prescribed regimen of medical, psychiatric, or psychological care or treatment.” The controlling opinion acknowledged a split with the First, Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Circuits, which have interpreted § 4243 and related statutes to permit recommitment of a person who violates a condition “ancillary” to those that are part of a prescribed regimen. Even under its narrower interpretation of § 4243, the Fourth Circuit panel majority held that revocation was proper because the condition the released individual violated (possessing a weapon) was part of a prescribed regimen prepared by the director of the mental health institution from which the individual was conditionally discharged (United States v. Roney).
Criminal Law & Procedure: In denying a prisoner’s motion to proceed in forma pauperis, the Fifth Circuit considered the meaning of 28 U.S.C. § 1915, which generally bars a prisoner from bringing a civil action or appealing a judgment in federal court without prepaying filing fees after three or more prior actions have been dismissed on enumerated grounds (sometimes called the “three strikes” rule). Here, the petitioner’s third “strike” was the lower court proceeding in the case before the circuit court—the petitioner sought to proceed in forma pauperis in appealing the lower court’s decision. The Fifth Circuit joined the Third Circuit in holding that the three strikes rule applies when the third strike itself is the subject of the appeal and disagreed with rulings by the Fourth and Ninth Circuits holding that prisoners may appeal their third strike in forma pauperis (Meeks v. Ray).
Criminal Law & Procedure: The Fifth Circuit largely affirmed a criminal defendant’s sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 2252A for committing a federal offense related to the receipt of child pornography, including a sentence enhancement because of a prior conviction under a Texas child pornography statute. A defendant convicted of a federal child pornography offense is subject to an enhanced minimum sentence under § 2252A(b)(1) if he or she had been convicted of a prior offense “relating to” the possession of child pornography, among other offenses. Although the defendant’s prior Texas conviction was for an offense that covered somewhat broader conduct than the federal child pornography statute, the Fifth Circuit joined the majority of reviewing circuits that have interpreted § 2252A(b)(1)’s “relating to” language to mean that the prior offense does not have to be a perfect match to the federal crime. The court acknowledged a split with the Sixth and Ninth Circuits, which have said that a sentencing enhancement under § 2252A(b)(1) is available only if the defendant’s prior state criminal law offense did not cover a broader swath of conduct than the federal child pornography offense (United States v. Mendoza).
Criminal Law & Procedure: On remand from the Supreme Court, the Eighth Circuit held that the Ex Post Facto Clause barred the application of the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act (MVRA), which extended the enforcement period for criminal restitution obligations under 18 U.S.C. § 3613(b), to criminal defendants whose offenses were committed before the MVRA’s enactment and for whom the restitution period would have expired if not for the MVRA. In reaching this conclusion, the Eighth Circuit joined the Third Circuit but split from at least two circuits (the Second and Ninth) that have held that the MVRA’s extension of the enforcement period would not implicate the Ex Post Facto Clause even when applied to defendants whose restitution period would have expired but for the MVRA (United States v. Ellingburg).
Elections: The Fourth Circuit held that a South Carolina statute authorizing absentee-by-mail voting without need provide a justification for not voting in person—but only for persons 65 years or older—violated the Twenty-Sixth Amendment. The Amendment provides that the right of U.S. citizens “who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age.” The South Carolina statute authorizes persons 65 years or older to cast absentee votes in any election for any reason (sometimes called “no-excuse” absentee voting), while persons under 65 may cast absentee ballots only if they satisfy specific statutory criteria. The Fourth Circuit held that the statute violated the Twenty-Sixth Amendment because it established different eligibility criteria for no-excuse absentee voting based on age. Although the state law did not make voting harder for persons under 65 years of age, the Fourth Circuit did not find this constitutionally significant; what mattered, according to the court, was that the law resulted in it being harder for persons under the age of 65 to vote than for persons 65 years or older. The panel acknowledged splits with the Fifth Circuit, which holds that an election law can only abridge one’s right to vote under the Twenty-Sixth Amendment if it makes it more difficult for a person to vote than before the law was enacted or enforced, and the Seventh Circuit, which looks to whether a material requirement meaningfully burdens the exercise of one’s voting rights (Grant v. Belangia).
Immigration: On a legal question the Supreme Court has agreed to take up this term, divided panels of the First and Third Circuits widened a circuit split over when an alien taken into immigration custody after unlawfully entering the country may be detained without bond during removal proceedings. Under federal statute, an alien often may be released from custody on bond or on the alien's own recognizance while removal proceedings are pending. Except in narrow circumstances, however, 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A) directs that, “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained [during removal proceedings]” (emphasis added). Federal statute provides that an alien “present in the United States who has not been admitted” shall be treated as an “applicant for admission,” but it does not define an “alien seeking admission.” The Fifth and Eighth Circuits have treated “applicant for admission” and “alien seeking admission” as synonymous, meaning that aliens present in the United States but not lawfully admitted are subject to mandatory detention under § 1225(b)(2)(A). A divided First Circuit disagreed, joining several other circuits—the Second, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh—that previously held that an “alien seeking admission” under § 1225(b)(2)(A) is not synonymous with an “applicant for admission,” and that § 1225(b)(2)(A) mandates detention only for unlawfully present aliens who are actively seeking lawful admission into the country. The First Circuit further held that the named alien petitioner’s application for cancellation of removal after being placed in removal proceedings did not mean he was “seeking admission” under § 1225(b)(2)(A). The court reasoned that the alien’s application for relief from removal was distinct from seeking lawful admission into the country. A few weeks later, a divided Third Circuit panel similarly held that § 1225(b)(2)(A) did not apply to aliens who entered the United States several years earlier and were not actively seeking admission into the United States. Unlike some other panels who decided similar challenges on statutory grounds, the Third Circuit panel majority also held that the mandatory detention of aliens who lived in the United States for extended periods and had no criminal records violated the Due Process Clause (First Circuit: Guerrero Orellana v. Moniz, Third Circuit: Buele Morocho v. Warden Philadelphia FDC). 
Immigration: The Fourth Circuit held that an alien was not inadmissible and removable from the United States on account of being “convicted of” an enumerated offense under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i) when the underlying conviction had been vacated. In so doing, the circuit panel rejected the long-standing interpretation of the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) and overturned circuit precedent that had afforded Chevron deference to the BIA’s interpretation. Under the BIA’s long-standing interpretation, a conviction vacated because of a substantive or procedural defect would not qualify as a conviction for immigration purposes but would qualify if vacated for any other reason. Because the Supreme Court in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled the Chevron doctrine that afforded judicial deference to agency interpretation of ambiguous statutes, the Fourth Circuit looked to the text of the statute and concluded that the best reading barred a vacated conviction from qualifying as a conviction for immigration purposes no matter the reason for the vacatur. In so doing, the court observed that it split from the First, Second, Third, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits, which agreed with the BIA’s position. The court also observed a split from the Fifth Circuit, which took the opposite view and held that a conviction always carries immigration consequences regardless of whether it is vacated (Yanez Piedra v. Blanche).
Immigration: A divided Fourth Circuit widened two separate circuit splits involving 8 U.S.C. § 1252, which governs judicial review of “final” orders of removal. The petitioner had a prior removal order reinstated after reentering the United States and, in administrative proceedings, was then denied withholding of removal under 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(3)(A) and relief under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). The petitioner conceded his removability under the reinstated removal order but sought review of his withholding and CAT claims under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(1), which grants federal appellate courts jurisdiction to review final orders of removal. Agreeing with the Third Circuit but disagreeing with the Ninth and Eleventh Circuits, the Fourth Circuit panel majority ruled that § 1252(a) did not deprive it of jurisdiction to review the denial of withholding of removal and CAT claims even when the petitioner did not challenge his underlying removability. The panel then considered whether the petitioner’s claims were time-barred. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1), a final order of removal must be appealed to a U.S. circuit court within 30 days. Here, the petitioner sought appellate review more than 30 days after his reinstated removal order but within 30 days of his request for CAT relief and withholding of removal being denied. After the petitioner filed his appeal, the Supreme Court, in Riley v. Bondi, held that the 30-day clock is tied to the final administrative order deciding that the alien is removable, not to the conclusion of any subsequent administrative proceedings concerning the alien’s eligibility for relief. The Fourth Circuit panel majority held that, under Riley, the statutory deadline for seeking appellate review was trigged by reinstatement of the petitioner’s removal order. Expressing disagreement with a Fifth Circuit opinion but endorsing the views of the Sixth and Seventh Circuits, the court held that § 1252(b)(1)’s deadline may be equitably tolled when the alien pursued his or her rights diligently and the delay resulted from extraordinary circumstances beyond the petitioner’s control. Such tolling allowed the court to consider the petitioner’s claim, the majority held, because his late filing was due to his reliance on judicial precedent abrogated by Riley. Turning to the merits, the majority vacated the administrative determination that the petitioner was ineligible for withholding of removal and CAT relief and remanded the case for further proceedings (Navarro Cerritos v. Blanche).
Securities: The Seventh Circuit affirmed a lower court’s dismissal of a lawsuit brought by investors who alleged that the defendant deceived the securities market through “channel stuffing,” a practice by which a seller foists inventory on distributors to create a false appearance of greater profitability. The plaintiffs brought claims under both the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the Exchange Act) and the Securities Act of 1933 (Securities Act). The Exchange Act claims were subject to the heightened pleading burden requirements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA) of 1995 for securities fraud claims brought by private parties. The circuit court concluded, among other things, that the plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the defendant’s actions gave rise to strong inference of an intent to deceive the market, a requisite under the PSLRA. Securities Act claims, in contrast, do not require proof of fraudulent intent, and the plaintiffs disclaimed any reliance on fraud for these claims in favor of negligence and strict liability. The circuit court nevertheless held that the plaintiffs were subject to an elevated pleading standard under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b), which imposes a higher burden for claims alleging fraud, and failed to meet that standard. The court explained that whether Rule 9(b) applies depends on the allegations of the complaint. The Seventh Circuit joined the Second, Third, Fourth, and Ninth Circuits—and parted ways with the Fifth and Eighth Circuits—to hold that, where plaintiffs rely on the same alleged course of conduct to bring securities fraud claims under the relevant portions of the Exchange Act and claims under the Securities Act, the allegations premised on fraud and the Securities Act claims are subject to Rule 9(b), notwithstanding plaintiffs’ express disavowal of fraud theories for those claims (Hunter v. Elanco Animal Health Inc.).
Securities: The Ninth Circuit affirmed a lower court’s dissolution of a preliminary injunction blocking Nevada from enforcing state gaming laws against Kalshi, a prediction markets platform. The circuit court agreed with the lower court that application of the Nevada gaming laws to Kalshi’s sport events contracts was likely not preempted by the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA). The CEA gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) exclusive jurisdiction over “transactions involving swaps . . . traded or executed on” a designated contract market (DCM). Although Kalshi is a regulated DCM and the Ninth Circuit agreed with Kalshi that the CEA expressly preempts state law regulating swaps traded on a DCM, the court held that Kalshi’s sports event contracts were not “swaps” under the CEA and so were subject to state regulation. The Ninth Circuit rejected the argument—which the Third Circuit had previously endorsed—that Kalshi’s sports events contracts met one part of the CEA’s definition of “swap,” which covers “any agreement . . . that provides for any purchase, sale, payment, or delivery . . . that is dependent on the occurrence, nonoccurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence” (emphasis added). The Ninth Circuit reasoned that the CEA’s context made clear that the definition of “swap” was intended to address financial risk-hedging interests and that Kalshi’s broader reading of “swap” to cover contracts predicting any “event” with potential financial consequences had no limiting principle and raised concerns under the major questions doctrine. The panel also ruled that 17 C.F.R. § 40.11(a), which bars a registered DCM from listing a contract that “involves, relates to, or references . . . gaming,” provided an additional basis to affirm the lower court’s ruling. (The CFTC has proposed revisions to the regulation that would remove this categorical prohibition.) The Ninth Circuit remanded the case to district court to consider in the first instance Nevada’s challenges to Kalshi’s contracts concerning elections. The Sixth Circuit has since deepened the circuit split by concluding that Kalshi’s sports event contracts are subject to state regulation on somewhat different grounds (KalshiEx, LLC v. Assad).
Separation of Powers: A divided Second Circuit affirmed a district court’s decision to quash grand jury subpoenas obtained by John Sarcone, the purported Acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York, after concluding he was not lawfully exercising the duties of that office. In July 2025, Sarcone was appointed as a “Special Attorney,” designated as the First Assistant U.S. Attorney (FAUSA) for the district, and authorized in that role to conduct “any kind of legal proceedings” that U.S. Attorneys “are authorized to conduct.” The Department of Justice (DOJ) claimed that, as the FAUSA, Sarcone could then serve as Acting U.S. Attorney pursuant to the Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998 (FVRA). The FVRA authorizes specific categories of officials to perform temporarily the functions and duties of certain vacant offices, including U.S. Attorney positions. As relevant here, the FVRA provides that if a covered officer “dies, resigns, or is otherwise unable to perform the functions and duties of the office, . . . the first assistant to the office of such officer shall perform the functions and duties of [that] office” for a prescribed period. The Second Circuit held that the FVRA only authorizes a first assistant to serve in an acting capacity if he or she was already in that role at the time the U.S. Attorney’s office became vacant. Among other factors, the court emphasized the “automaticity” of the statutory text, ruling that it operates at the time the vacancy occurs. The DOJ argued in the alternative that it had lawfully delegated subpoena authority to Sarcone in his roles as First Assistant and Special Attorney. The panel majority rejected this argument, holding that, because the FVRA states that it is “the exclusive means for temporarily authorizing” acting service, the law barred the “wholesale delegation” of the U.S. Attorney’s functions to Sarcone. The panel majority’s interpretation of the FVRA is consistent with Third and Ninth Circuit rulings on Acting U.S. Attorneys in New Jersey and Nevada. All three circuits, however, disagreed with an earlier decision of the Federal Circuit that had concluded the FVRA did not bar such a delegation (In re Grand Jury Subpoenas to the Off. of the N.Y. Att’y Gen.).

api_metadata.summary:
Under federal law, cannabis and its derivatives are classified as either marijuana or hemp. Marijuana is subject to regulation under the federal Controlled Substances Act (CSA), while hemp is not a controlled substance. The CSA also separately regulates tetrahydrocannabinols (THC), other than “[THC] in hemp.” While hemp and THC in hemp are not controlled substances, they may be regulated by other provisions of federal law, such as agricultural laws and the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
In November 2025, a provision of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 (Pub. L. No. 119-37) (Hemp Definition Amendment) amended the definition of hemp to expressly exclude certain substances and include other hemp-derived products. The new hemp definition was originally scheduled to go into effect on November 12, 2026, but a provision of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (Pub. L. No. 119-103) (Delay Amendment) delayed the effective date for most of the amendments to the hemp definition until December 11, 2026. The Delay Amendment allows certain provisions of the new hemp definition to go into effect as planned on November 12, 2026—the provisions excluding products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant. This Legal Sidebar provides background on the federal regulation of hemp and marijuana and an overview of the new hemp definition. It then discusses the legal status of cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant. Finally, it concludes with some considerations for Congress.
Background
The plant cannabis sativa and its derivatives are used for a variety of medical, recreational, and industrial purposes. Certain compounds found in cannabis or related to compounds in cannabis, known as cannabinoids, may have physiological or psychoactive effects. The most well-known types of cannabinoids are THC and cannabidiol (CBD). CBD is not intoxicating, while THC is psychoactive and produces the “high” associated with marijuana. There are multiple types of THC. Delta-9 THC is the primary psychoactive cannabinoid found in the cannabis plant. Other forms of THC include delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC, and THC acetate ester (THC-O). Some types of THC occur naturally in the cannabis plant, while others do not. The chemical processes required to isolate or produce sufficient quantities of THC to use vary depending on the type of THC. For instance, THC-O does not occur naturally in cannabis and is produced from the plant by converting cannabis-derived CBD to delta-8 THC, then adding acetic anhydride. Although different varieties of the cannabis plant have different primary uses, cannabis has long been used for its psychoactive effects by smoking or otherwise ingesting the plant or its derivatives, while the plant’s stalks and fibers are used in a range of products including textiles, spun fibers, paper, and construction and insulation materials. Increasingly, entities are extracting specific cannabinoids and isolating or chemically manipulating them to introduce them into a wide array of consumer products. Some of these products are non-intoxicating products like CBD oil, while others may have intoxicating effects. 
Under federal law, cannabis and its derivatives generally fall into one of two categories: marijuana or hemp. Currently, unless an exception applies, cannabis and its derivatives are legally classified as marijuana, which is a controlled substance under the federal CSA. Beginning when Congress enacted the CSA in 1970, marijuana was classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, meaning it was subject to the most stringent CSA restrictions and could not legally be used for medical or recreational purposes. In April 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) issued a final order moving marijuana and its derivatives to Schedule III to the extent they are “included in an FDA-approved drug product or are subject to a state-issued license to manufacture, distribute, and/or dispense marijuana or products containing marijuana for medical purposes” (state-legal medical marijuana). The rescheduling of state-legal medical marijuana may allow marijuana to be used for medical purposes consistent with the CSA. DOJ is also considering whether to move all marijuana to Schedule III but, for the time being, marijuana other than state-regulated medical marijuana remains in Schedule I. Both Schedule I and Schedule III status impose regulatory requirements for legal activities involving marijuana, and unauthorized activities are subject to significant criminal penalties.
One key exception to the general classification of cannabis as marijuana applies to cannabis that fits the legal definition of hemp. The 2018 farm bill defined hemp as any part of the cannabis plant or its derivatives containing no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC and excluded hemp from the definition of marijuana under the CSA. Thus, after enactment of the 2018 farm bill, hemp is no longer a controlled substance under the CSA. 
THC is separately classified as a Schedule I controlled substance under the CSA, unless an exception applies. CSA control of THC includes THC that naturally occurs in the plant and synthetic equivalents of those substances, as well as their derivatives and isomers. The 2018 farm bill amended the statute controlling THC in Schedule I to exclude “[THC] in hemp.” This amendment excludes substances that meet the definition of hemp implemented by the 2018 farm bill from the classification of THC as a Schedule I controlled substance. 
Following enactment of the 2018 farm bill, some participants in the cannabis industry began producing products that contain less than 0.3% delta-9 THC but have a total THC concentration that exceeds 0.3%. As a result of the total THC concentration, these products may be intoxicating to the user. Due to the low delta-9 THC concentration, however, these products may legally qualify as hemp and be exempt from CSA restrictions that apply to marijuana and THC. Critics of the proliferation of these THC products dubbed this interpretation of the 2018 farm bill the “THC loophole.” 
The New Hemp Definition
In November 2025, Congress enacted and the President signed the Hemp Definition Amendment, which amended the definition of hemp from the 2018 farm bill. The new definition of hemp includes cannabis and its derivatives “with a total [THC] concentration” of not more than 0.3%. The amendment addresses the so-called “THC loophole” because the threshold concentration in the new definition is based on total THC concentration (including delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC, and THC-O), rather than only on the concentration of delta-9 THC.
The amended hemp definition expressly includes “industrial hemp” grown for purposes of producing non-cannabinoid products including stalks, fibers, whole grains, oils, and edible greens. It also enumerates certain exclusions from the definition of hemp:
viable seeds from a cannabis plant if the plant exceeds a total THC concentration of 0.3%;
hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant;
hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing cannabinoids that are capable of being naturally produced by a cannabis plant and were synthesized or manufactured outside the plant;
intermediate hemp-derived products containing more than 0.3% total THC and other cannabinoids that have similar effects as a [THC]; and
final hemp-derived products with greater than 0.4 milligrams combined total per container of total THC and other cannabinoids that have similar effects as a [THC].
The Hemp Definition Amendment defines intermediate hemp-derived cannabinoid product in part as a hemp-derived cannabinoid product that “is not yet in the final form” intended to be used or consumed by humans or animals. It does not separately define final hemp-derived cannabinoid product, but the phrase appears to refer to hemp-derived cannabinoid products in the final form intended to be used by humans or animals.
The Hemp Definition Amendment also directs the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), within 90 days of enactment, to publish lists of
all cannabinoids known to FDA that can be naturally produced by a cannabis plant;
all THC class cannabinoids known to the agency to occur naturally in the plant;
all other known cannabinoids with similar effects to, or marketed to have similar effects to, THC class cannabinoids; and
“additional information and specificity” about the term “container.”
As of the date of the publication of this Legal Sidebar, FDA has not published any of these items. 
The Hemp Definition Amendment originally provided that the amendment was to take effect one year from the date of enactment, on November 12, 2026. In September 2026, Congress enacted the Delay Amendment, which delayed the effective date for most of the amendments to the hemp definition until December 11, 2026. Certain provisions regarding the exclusion for hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant remain set to go into effect on November 12, 2026. On that date, hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing cannabinoids not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant will not be classified as hemp, and will be treated as controlled substances to the extent they fall within the CSA’s definition of marijuana or THC. 
Legal Status of Cannabinoids That Do Not Naturally Occur in Cannabis
Hemp-derived cannabis products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant are the subject of two contradictory conclusions regarding their legal status: the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration’s (DEA’s) interpretation of the 2018 farm bill’s hemp definition, which appears to categorize cannabinoids that do not naturally occur in the cannabis plant as controlled substances; and an appeals court opinion, Anderson v. Diamondback Investment Group, which categorized certain cannabinoids that do not naturally occur in cannabis as hemp, and not controlled substances.
DEA Interpretation of the 2018 Farm Bill’s Hemp Provision
On August 20, 2020, DEA issued an interim final rule to explain how the 2018 farm bill’s descheduling of hemp affected the Schedule I status of THC. The interim final rule states that the 2018 farm bill “limits the control” of THC that is “naturally occurring” in hemp. According to DEA, the 2018 farm bill “does not impact the control status of synthetically derived [THC] because the statutory definition of hemp’ is limited to materials that are derived” from the cannabis plant. For products with “synthetically derived” THC, the amount of delta-9 THC “is not a determining factor in whether the material is a controlled substance” because “[a]ll synthetically derived [THCs] remain schedule I controlled substances.”
In an opinion letter issued on February 13, 2023, DEA addressed the status of THC-O. In the letter, DEA opined that THC-O—a compound that does not occur naturally in the cannabis plant—is a Schedule I controlled substance because it “can only be obtained synthetically, and therefore [does] not fall under the definition of hemp.” The 2023 letter focused on whether or not the cannabinoid naturally occurs in cannabis, rather than whether or not the cannabinoid was derived from cannabis materials. 
Anderson v. Diamondback Investment Group
On September 4, 2024, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit (Fourth Circuit) issued an opinion in Anderson v. Diamondback Investment Group that contradicts DEA’s 2023 opinion letter on THC-O by holding that products containing THC-O were hemp.
In Anderson, the defendant employer fired the plaintiff from her job for failing two drug tests. The plaintiff claimed, among other things, that her firing violated a North Carolina law that prohibited an employer from terminating an employee for engaging “in the lawful use of lawful products.” The Fourth Circuit considered whether the products that the plaintiff consumed—which included CBD oil, delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC, and THC-O—were legally hemp, and therefore not subject to the CSA, under the 2018 farm bill. The Fourth Circuit held that the 2018 farm bill definition unambiguously establishes that “hemp” includes “all” cannabinoids, and derivatives and extracts of cannabis, so long as they do not cross the 0.3% delta-9 THC threshold. According to the court, whether a substance is considered hemp does not depend on how it was manufactured but rather whether it comes from cannabis. The court also noted that, in light of the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright v. Raimondo overturning the Chevron doctrine, it would not need to defer to DEA’s interpretation even if the court had determined that the statutory definition was ambiguous. In coming to this conclusion, the court relied on AK Futures v. Boyd Street Distro, in which the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit opined that products containing Delta-8 THC (which, unlike THC-O, does naturally occur in hemp) were hemp because the cannabinoid was derived from the cannabis plant. According to the Fourth Circuit, a product containing THC-O that was derived from cannabis is hemp under the 2018 farm bill’s definition so long as it does not contain more than 0.3% delta-9 THC. Synthetic cannabinoids, the court opined, were “compounds manufactured entirely out of synthetic materials.”
Considerations for Congress
To the extent the Hemp Definition Amendment goes into effect, it will amend the definition of hemp to exclude certain products, meaning that some additional products containing THC will be subject to control under the CSA by the DEA. In response, some hemp industry groups have expressed opposition to the definitional changes, preferring regulation of hemp-derived consumer products through agencies like FDA. These stakeholders have generally supported delaying the effective date for the new hemp definition to extend the time for Congress to decide whether to pass a separate regulatory framework for hemp products. Other stakeholders, including several state attorneys general, have opposed the delay in the effective date of the new hemp definition, citing the need to protect consumers. 
The Delay Amendment did not change the effective date excluding from the hemp definition products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant. This provision will categorize certain products that contain cannabinoids that are derived from hemp but do not naturally occur in hemp, such as THC-O, as controlled substances under the CSA. Congress may consider further delaying the effective date of any or all parts of the new hemp definition. Some Members of Congress have introduced legislation that would delay the effective date of the new definition of hemp for an additional two years (H.R. 7024, H.R. 7010, S. 3686) or repeal the changes to the definition (H.R. 6209). Congress may also allow the new hemp definition to take effect. 
To the extent hemp-derived cannabinoid products are classified as marijuana, any change to CSA regulation of marijuana would also apply to those products. As noted, in April 2026, DOJ moved state-legal medical marijuana to Schedule III, and the agency is currently considering whether to reschedule the substance entirely. As of the date of this Legal Sidebar, marijuana other than state-legal medical marijuana remains in Schedule I. Congress has broad authority to change the status of a controlled substance through legislation and could change the status of marijuana before or after DEA makes any final scheduling decision. Congress could choose to act with respect to marijuana generally or with respect to hemp-derived cannabinoid products in particular. For more legal considerations related to the implementation of the new federal definition of hemp, see CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11381, Changes to the Federal Definition of Hemp: Legal Considerations Under the Controlled Substances Act, by Joanna R. Lampe (2025).
