api_metadata.summary:
When federal agencies and programs do not receive funding after full-year or interim appropriations expire, they experience a “funding gap.” If funding does not resume in time to continue government operations, the government generally begins a “shutdown” of affected activities. Shutdowns can be government-wide or partial (i.e., affecting certain federal agencies and programs) depending on which appropriations lapse.
The federal government plays a key role in operating the National Airspace System, providing air traffic control and air navigation services, and conducting aviation security operations at the nation’s airports. Shutdowns can affect some civil aviation programs that are administered by the Department of Transportation (DOT), mostly those managed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), as well as aviation security functions carried out by other federal entities, particularly the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). 
Shutdowns over the past decade have been lengthier than those during previous lapses in appropriations and have directly impacted civil aviation operations. Federal workers who perform functions integral to these civil aviation operations are generally excepted from furlough during shutdowns. These workers typically are not paid during a shutdown, which has demonstrated impacts on absenteeism and resignations, potentially affecting the federal government’s ability to provide full aviation services without disruption or degradation. Quantifiable indicators of these impacts include increased flight delays and cancellations, extended wait times at airport security checkpoints, temporary FAA-mandated flight reductions at major U.S. airports, and forgone revenues for airlines, airports, and related businesses. 
Some Members of Congress introduced bills that would have ensured the continuation of aviation operations until funding through normal appropriations was restored during the lapses in FY2026. Some of those bills in the 119th Congress focused on the use of continuing appropriations to pay essential government workers or, specifically, essential FAA and TSA personnel during shutdowns; others proposed to establish certain types of automatic continuing resolutions that would provide a fallback funding source for core aviation safety operations in the event of future funding gaps. Other bills seek a more permanent solution for aviation security functions. For example, the Pay TSA Act of 2026 (H.R. 7941) proposes the creation of a dedicated trust fund that would be funded by passenger security fees and available to expend during a lapse in appropriations. Language in H.R. 7941 expressly prioritizes the use of money in the fund during a shutdown for salaries, benefits, and overtime compensation for TSA screeners; maintenance of staffing levels at aviation security screening checkpoints; and other operational expenses directly supporting frontline aviation security personnel. Some Members may wish to leave in place the balance between the continuation of government services and the congressional power of the purse that exists during a shutdown.

api_metadata.summary:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA; S. 5653) was introduced on September 30, 2026. The bill as introduced contains seven titles within two divisions, which aim to reform certain federal environmental review and permitting processes to expedite a wide range of project types, with an emphasis on energy-related projects. 
Some Members have shown sustained interest over several Congresses in amending the nation’s permitting laws to increase energy production and expedite a variety of projects (e.g., transportation infrastructure, energy, data center development, ecological restoration, stormwater infrastructure). Some Members have introduced numerous permitting-reform-related bills, some of which have focused on specific environmental statutes with review and/or permitting provisions (e.g., the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Historic Preservation Act). Others have focused on specific project types (e.g., electricity transmission lines, natural gas pipelines, geothermal energy development), and some have included broader reforms to permitting and reviews across project types.
Areas of debate on previous legislative proposals have included whether reforms should target conventional or renewable forms of energy, whether amending bedrock environmental laws to shorten reviews may weaken environmental protections, and whether certain proposals may narrow the role of states in the review process and/or reduce opportunities for public input and judicial review.
BAAJA is the product of negotiations involving Members of the Senate Committees on Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources. In a majority press release announcing the introduction of the bill, the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources asserted that the legislation “will strengthen American energy security by accelerating the permitting process for critical energy and mineral projects across the United States.” A majority press release from the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works stated that the agreement “will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.”
This report analyzes the provisions in BAAJA specific to the Clean Water Act (CWA, Division A, Title II). Section 1201 would formally require the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to issue water quality criteria through notice and comment rulemaking. It would specify the judicial review provision applicable to issuance of water quality criteria and regulations defining the scope of “waters of the United States.” Section 1202 would amend CWA Section 401 to narrow the scope of what certifying authorities (typically states) can consider in their water quality certification reviews and the scope of conditions they could include when granting certifications generally. It would further narrow the scope of certification reviews and conditions for certain projects, including interstate transmission line and natural gas pipeline projects. It would also narrow the bases on which certification may be denied and would amend several aspects of Section 401 certification timelines, processes, and judicial review. Section 1203 would extend the permit term limit for National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits from 5 years to 10 years. Section 1204 would limit the period of time during which EPA could issue a Section 404(c) “veto” of a Section 404 permit for the discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States. It would extend the permit term limits for Section 404 general permits from 5 years to 10 years. It would specify that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) consideration of environmental effects for general permits be limited to water quality requirements, which is newly defined in the bill, and that any adverse effects of discharges of dredge or fill material into less than 2 acres of waters of the United States are considered minimal. It would require USACE to maintain certain nationwide permits and would raise the threshold of allowable impacts for coverage under these permits. Section 1205 would impose a 150-day statute of limitations for lawsuits challenging Section 404 permits and certain other actions taken pursuant to Section 404. It would limit the availability of judicial review to parties that commented on an issue related to the lawsuit during the public comment period. It would limit the ability of courts to vacate permits or agency actions found to be unlawful and would require courts to set and enforce specific deadlines for agencies to act on remand.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) started its hate crime statistics program pursuant to the Hate Crime Statistics Act of 1990 (HCSA; P.L. 101-275). The HCSA directs the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) to acquire and report data on crimes that “manifest evidence of prejudice based on race, gender and gender identity, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or ethnicity, including where appropriate the crimes of murder, non-negligent manslaughter; forcible rape; aggravated assault, simple assault, intimidation; arson; and destruction, damage or vandalism of property.” These data are collected by the local, state, federal, and tribal law enforcement agencies to which the offenses were reported and submitted to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) program. 
Hate Crime Victimization Rates by Data Source, 2015-2024
/
Source: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Crime Data Explorer, https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/webapp/#/pages/downloads (accessed August 29, 2025); and Bureau of Justice Statistics, National Crime Victimization Survey, https://bjs.ojp.gov/data-collection/ncvs.
Notes: The NCVS estimates are based on the non-institutionalized U.S. resident population age 12 or older. The shaded region is the 95% confidence interval.
In addition to the FBI’s hate crime data collection efforts, the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) collects data on hate crime victimizations as part of the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS). NCVS respondents self-report their personal experiences with certain non-fatal crimes (e.g., robbery, aggravated assault) and, among responses to many other questions, whether they believe their criminal victimization was bias-motivated. In contrast to the FBI’s data, NCVS victimizations include incidents that were reported and not reported to the police. This report presents analyses of hate crime data collected from 2015 to 2024 by both the FBI and NCVS. 
Both the UCR and NCVS data indicate that hate crime rates have generally increased from 2015 to 2024. The UCR hate crime data show an 89% increase in the police-verified hate crime victimization rate over this 10-year period, rising from 1.8 hate crime victimizations per 100,000 people in 2015 to 3.4 per 100,000 in 2024. Similarly, the NCVS data show a 225% increase over this same 10-year period, rising from 55 self-reported hate crime victimizations per 100,000 people in 2015 to 179 per 100,000 in 2024. This trend of increasing hate crime rates observed in both datasets contrasts with current trends in non-bias-motivated crime rates, which have been generally decreasing in recent years.
The UCR and NCVS hate crime data show that most reported victimizations from 2015 to 2024 were motivated by race/ethnicity/ancestry. This was the bias category for 62.7% of victimizations reported in the UCR and 66.3% of victimizations reported in the NCVS. Other common bias categories were sexual orientation, religion, and gender identity. The UCR, but not the NCVS, reports more specific bias motivations within these broader categories. From 2015 to 2024, 51.0% of the 56,512 race/ethnicity/ancestry-motivated victimizations in the UCR data were anti-Black/African American, 56.9% of the 17,074 sexual-orientation-motivated offenses were anti-gay (male), 54.9% of the 13,098 religion-motivated offenses were anti-Jewish, and 78.3% of the 3,049 gender-identity-motivated offenses were anti-transgender.

The federal fleet of oceanographic research vessels serves as a primary tool for advancing knowledge of the ocean system. The federal oceanographic fleet is primarily composed of oceanographic research vessels that are owned and operated or leased by federal departments and agencies. Federally funded projects have included the mapping of the seafloor, which aids in the delineation of the outer limits of U.S. maritime boundaries; the identification and study of marine resources for protection, management, or exploitation; ocean exploration; U.S. Arctic and Antarctic research; and U.S. ocean-based research broadly, including the installation, removal, and maintenance of U.S. ocean observation networks. Some of these activities also contribute to various national security objectives. At issue for Congress is understanding the current capacity of the federal oceanographic fleet and its future capability to support ocean research and related national security priorities in a timely and cost-effective manner.
In March 2016, the Interagency Working Group on Facilities and Infrastructure (IWG-FI) published a federal oceanographic research vessel status report entitled Federal Fleet Status Report: Current Capacity and Near-Term Priorities. In this report, the IWG-FI inventoried the oceanographic research vessels that composed the federal fleet at the end of FY2015. The 2016 federal fleet status report also provided an outlook of the fleet’s capacity through FY2030 and discussed the potential impacts associated with changes to capacity. The IWG-FI, a non-congressionally mandated working group that is cochaired by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Department of Navy, has not published a federal fleet status report since 2016. 
The 2016 federal fleet status report included vessels owned and operated or leased by NOAA, the Department of the Navy, the National Science Foundation, and the U.S. Coast Guard. Since the publication of the 2016 fleet status report, several oceanographic research vessels have retired from the fleet, entered into the fleet, or required maintenance to extend their service lives. The IWG-FI began preparing a new updated federal fleet status report in 2023. In 2024, NOAA acknowledged that an update to the 2016 federal fleet status report was being prepared, but the agency provided no timeline for its publication. To date, the 2016 report remains the most comprehensive publicly available assessment of the federal oceanographic fleet.
Congressional decisionmaking on the federal oceanographic fleet can substantially affect federal agencies’ abilities to fulfill their missions (e.g., science and research, education, and navigation safety) and the fleet’s ability to address certain national security concerns. Recurring status reports about the federal oceanographic fleet could inform congressional deliberation over and decisions related to the fleet. Congress could pursue several options for mandating reporting on the federal fleet status; in doing so, it could specify the report’s contents. For example, Congress could direct the report to inventory the fleet at the time of publication; provide additional details about agencies’ future plans, including funding needs to maintain, expand, or reduce the fleet’s size to meet evolving congressional priorities; or both. Alternatively, Congress could choose to maintain the status quo and defer to the executive branch on whether, and if so when and how, to update the federal fleet status report.
Given that oceanographic research vessels are a shared federal asset, improved collaboration among federal agencies might allow the government to reduce the number of vessels in the fleet and thus reduce operational costs. Congress has directed federal agencies to increase their use of uncrewed marine systems (UMSs) as a cost-cutting measure. While deploying a UMS may cost less than deploying an oceanographic research vessel, some UMSs would need to be deployed from a vessel. 
Congress also may be interested in understanding how the size, capabilities, and utilization of the U.S. oceanographic research fleet compare to the fleets of foreign governments (e.g., the People’s Republic of China [PRC] and/or Russia). Some Members of Congress are concerned about the PRC’s expanding global deployment of its state-owned fleet of oceanographic research vessels. Several stakeholders have expressed concerns about how data collected by PRC oceanographic research vessels may present national security concerns, as these data have numerous applications, including for military use. Congress could examine whether the current U.S. oceanographic research fleet is capable of collecting these types of data and whether the United States should consider oceanographic research vessels for national security objectives, in addition to research activities. Such an examination may elucidate congressional priorities for the renewal of the federal oceanographic research fleet.

Decommissioning offshore oil and gas platforms and related infrastructure generally means removing these facilities from the seafloor, permanently plugging all wells, plugging or removing pipelines, clearing the seafloor of obstructions, and taking related actions associated with the end of oil and gas production from an offshore lease. Pursuant to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA; 43 U.S.C. §§1331-1356c), the Department of the Interior (DOI) has issued decommissioning regulations for oil and gas operators on the U.S. outer continental shelf (OCS). Regulating OCS decommissioning has posed challenges for DOI’s ocean energy management agencies—the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), which are being merged into a new DOI agency called the Marine Minerals Administration. 
Although DOI’s regulations and lease provisions make offshore oil and gas lessees responsible for infrastructure decommissioning, lessees have not always fulfilled their decommissioning responsibilities. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that, of roughly 1,600 platforms and 8,000 wells existing in the Gulf of Mexico (now Gulf of America) at that time, more than 500 platforms and 2,700 wells were overdue for decommissioning under DOI regulations. In some cases, offshore operators have been unable to meet their decommissioning responsibilities—for instance, due to bankruptcy—leaving the federal government responsible for decommissioning such so-called orphaned infrastructure. Financial bonds required by DOI from offshore operators to cover decommissioning costs have not been sufficient to cover all liability in such cases.
Congress and successive presidential Administrations have considered how to address offshore decommissioning needs and how to reduce federal financial liability for decommissioning. Some approaches have involved changes to DOI’s financial assurance and supplemental bonding regulations. Other approaches have considered ways to reduce lessees’ decommissioning costs, especially through options for decommissioning in place. Under these approaches, lessees do not need to fully remove all infrastructure, but can leave some structures on the seafloor to serve various purposes. A prominent existing framework for decommissioning in place is the Rigs-to-Reefs program, under which some structures may remain in the ocean to serve as artificial reefs for marine life. Some Members of Congress and other stakeholders seek to grow this program, citing potential enhancements to fisheries and some marine industries, while others question whether the structures could pose environmental or navigational hazards. Other potential uses for legacy offshore infrastructure, such as repurposing for other offshore energy development, offshore aquaculture, or sea-based space launches, also have been proposed. In a regulatory agenda published in August 2026, DOI announced a proposal to make toppling in place (one method of decommissioning in place) the default standard for OCS infrastructure, under specified circumstances. Also, in September 2026, President Trump issued an executive order, “Restoring American Saltwater Angling and Recreation,” which among other provisions directed DOI to establish a program to facilitate conversion of decommissioned offshore oil and gas and other-use structures into permanent artificial reefs through a variety of reefing methods.
Congress may continue to consider how to address economic and environmental issues related to offshore decommissioning and whether to promote alternatives to full infrastructure removal. Bills under consideration in the 119th Congress would address decommissioning enforcement (H.R. 8099, S. 4239), offshore lessees’ financial strength and bonding requirements (H.R. 9034, H.R. 9035, S. 4715), federal appropriations for decommissioning activities (H.R. 9171), and artificial reefing and the Rigs-to-Reefs program (H.R. 5745).

House procedures are based not only on the rules the chamber adopts at the start of each Congress but also on constitutional mandates, published precedents, rulemaking statutes, procedural principles detailed in Jefferson’s Manual, and informal practices. In addition, House committee and party rules may influence House procedures. 
Various reference sources contain the text of the different parliamentary authorities that establish the parameters by which the House conducts its business. These resources provide insight into the daily proceedings of the House, and it may be necessary to review a combination of sources to understand specific procedural situations. 
Among the resources available to Members and their staff, four may be especially useful to understanding and following House procedure: House Practice, the House Manual, Deschler’s Precedents, and resolutions containing “special rules” from the House Committee on Rules. 
House Practice presents information about contemporary procedure in the House. It includes chapters that summarize House practice on topics such as amendments, points of order, and voting. House Practice is often a good place to begin research into House procedure because it contains numerous references to other procedural authorities such as the rules and selected precedents. It can be found via govinfo.gov, a website of the Government Publishing Office, at https://www.govinfo.gov/collection/house-practice?path=/GPO/House%20Practice, or through Congress.gov, a website of the Library of Congress, at https://www.congress.gov/help/house-of-representatives. 
The House Manual sets forth the main procedural authorities of the House, including the Constitution, portions of Jefferson’s Manual, the adopted rules of the House, and provisions of statutes with procedural effects. The different authorities are accompanied by the Parliamentarian’s annotations, which include citations to precedents interpreting those provisions. The current version of the House Manual can be accessed through govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/HMAN-119/pdf/HMAN-119.pdf, or via Congress.gov at https://www.congress.gov/help/house-of-representatives.
Deschler’s Precedents presents and summarizes significant precedents of the House established at various points of time since 1936. This series of 18 volumes often provides the text of the procedural exchange during which each precedent was established. Deschler’s Precedents is available through govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/collection/precedents-of-the-house?path=/gpo/Precedents%20of%20the%20U.S.%20House%20of%20Representatives/010-Deschler%27s%20Precedents and Congress.gov at https://www.congress.gov/help/house-of-representatives.
Following the completion of Deschler’s Precedents, the Office of the Parliamentarian began to publish a new series of House precedents, titled Precedents of the United States House of Representatives. The series will focus on contemporary developments in House procedure. The first three volumes are available through govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/collection/precedents-of-the-house?path=/gpo/Precedents%20of%20the%20U.S.%20House%20of%20Representatives/ and Congress.gov at https://www.congress.gov/help/house-of-representatives.
The House often adopts simple resolutions (“special rules”) that establish the floor procedures for considering one or more measures. These special rules may, for example, identify which amendments to a measure are in order and who may offer those amendments. Resolutions containing these special rules are reported from the Committee on Rules and made available on their website at https://rules.house.gov/, and through Congress.gov at https://www.congress.gov/.
House rules require each standing committee to adopt its own rules of procedure. The House Committee on Rules prepares a catalog of all House committee rules for each Congress titled Rules Adopted by the Committees of the House of Representatives. The version prepared for the 119th Congress is available via govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CPRT-119HPRT60630/pdf/CPRT-119HPRT60630.pdf.

The Senate’s procedures are determined not only by its standing rules but also by standing orders, published precedents, committee rules, party conference rules, and informal practices. The Constitution and rulemaking statutes also impose procedural requirements on the Senate. 
Official parliamentary reference documents and other publications set forth the text of the various authorities or provide information about how and when they govern different procedural situations. Together, these sources establish the parameters by which the Senate conducts its business. They provide insight into the Senate’s daily proceedings, which can be unpredictable. In order to understand Senate procedure, it is often necessary to consider more than one source of authority. For example, the Senate’s standing rules provide for the presiding officer to recognize the first Senator who seeks recognition on the floor. By precedent, however, when several Senators seek recognition at the same time, the majority leader is recognized first, followed by the minority leader. This precedent may have consequences for action on the floor. 
Among the resources available to Senators and their staff, four may prove especially useful to understand the Senate’s daily order of business: the Senate Manual, Riddick’s Senate Procedure, the rules of the Senate standing committees, and the publication of unanimous consent agreements. 
The Senate sets forth its chief procedural authorities in a Senate document called the Senate Manual (S.Doc. 118-1), a new edition of which appears periodically. The Manual contains the text of the Senate’s standing rules, permanent standing orders, laws relating to the Senate, and the Constitution, all of which establish key Senate procedures. The most recent version of the Manual can be accessed online at govinfo.gov, a website of the Government Publishing Office (GPO), at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SMAN-118/pdf/SMAN-118.pdf. It is also accessible via the Senate resources page of Congress.gov, a website of the Library of Congress, at https://www.congress.gov/resources/display/content/Senate. 
Riddick’s Senate Procedure (S.Doc. 101-28) presents a catalog of Senate precedents arranged alphabetically on topics ranging from adjournment to recognition to voting. Summaries of the precedents are accompanied by citations to the page and date in the Congressional Record or the Senate Journal on which the precedent was established. Individual chapters of Riddick’s Senate Procedure are available for download through govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/GPO-RIDDICK-1992. A searchable version is also accessible via the Senate resources page of Congress.gov at https://www.congress.gov/resources/display/content/Senate.
The Senate’s standing rules require each standing committee to adopt its own rules of procedure. These rules may cover topics such as proxy voting, quorum requirements, and the preparation of committee reports. Each Congress, the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration prepares a compilation of these rules and other relevant committee materials, such as jurisdiction information, in a document titled Authority and Rules of Senate Committees. The most recent version (S.Doc. 118-4) is available via govinfo.gov at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CDOC-118sdoc4/pdf/CDOC-118sdoc4.pdf. Each committee’s rules appear in the Congressional Record on the day they are submitted for publication, and many committees post them on their websites. 
To facilitate the legislative process, the Senate often conducts its business through unanimous consent agreements that may schedule the time for taking up a measure or specify what motions are in order during its consideration. These can be found, via Congress.gov, in the Congressional Record at https://www.congress.gov/ and the Senate Calendar of Business or the Executive Calendar at https://www.congress.gov/calendars-and-schedules.

The Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan is an important U.S. partner in the Middle East, and the two countries have cooperated closely for decades. Issues of bilateral cooperation include countering Islamist extremism, stabilizing Iraq and Syria, promoting the Israeli-Palestinian peace process, and thwarting Iranian regional influence. Security cooperation is arguably the foundation of the U.S.-Jordanian relationship. The United States also is a significant contributor of foreign assistance to Jordan and has provided aid to key sectors, such as the kingdom’s water distribution system.
During the 2026 U.S.-Iran conflict, Jordan and the U.S. forces it hosts have been targeted. As of September 2026, Iran had fired over 400 projectiles at Jordan. In July 2026, three American soldiers were killed when Iranian missiles struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base (MSAB), a Jordanian facility used by U.S. Air Forces Central Command (AFCENT).
Jordan’s long-standing policy toward Israel and the Palestinians has been to maintain its 1994 peace treaty with Israel while supporting a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict that would ultimately lead to an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is a pivotal issue in Jordanian politics. Though Jordan and Israel remain peaceful neighbors and continue to cooperate quietly on security issues, long-standing animosity between Jordan’s King Abdullah II and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with broader Jordanian opposition to Israel’s policies in the West Bank, has strained bilateral relations.
Over decades, U.S. assistance has helped Jordan address serious vulnerabilities, both internal and external. Jordan’s small size, refugee burden, and lack of major economic resources have made it dependent on aid from various Western and Arab sources. Between FY1951 and FY2026, the United States provided approximately $35.5 billion in foreign assistance to Jordan, making it one of the top recipients of U.S. aid globally. 
On September 16, 2022, the United States and Jordan signed their fourth Memorandum of Understanding governing U.S. foreign aid to Jordan. The seven-year agreement (FY2023-FY2029), subject to appropriations of Congress, commits the Administration to seeking $1.45 billion in annual economic and military aid for Jordan. Proposed legislation for FY2027 would increase that amount.
H.R. 8595, the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027, would provide a total of $2.1 billion in foreign aid to Jordan. H.R. 9495, the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2027, would provide “not less than” $150 million in defense appropriations for Jordanian border security and “up to” $500 million to support the armed forces of Jordan. S. 4784, the Senate’s National Defense Authorization bill, contains Section 1201, which would authorize U.S. defense assistance to the Jordanian Armed Forces through 2027 to secure Jordan’s borders, increase Middle East stability, counter terrorism and Iranian-supported groups, and improve interoperability with U.S. forces. The bill also would require prior congressional notification before assistance is provided.

api_metadata.summary:
The Senate generally cedes to its majority leader the prerogative of calling up items of business for floor consideration. Most measures are brought to the floor by unanimous consent, but when this consent cannot be obtained, a motion to proceed to consider can be used to accomplish the same purpose. Sometimes a Senator other than the majority leader offers this motion, but usually this occurs in coordination with the majority leader. Any Senator may be recognized to offer the motion to proceed, but in practice—perhaps on account of the wide range of procedural prerogatives they all enjoy during floor consideration—Senators generally defer to the majority leader in scheduling the business of the Senate.
The motion to proceed in the Senate may be applied to executive business (nominations or treaties) or to items of legislative business, the latter of which are the focus here. Motions to proceed to legislative business are normally debatable unless the underlying measure is “privileged,” which includes conference reports and measures subject to statutory expedited procedures. In some cases, more than one motion to proceed may be offered on the same measure.
Of the 866 motions to proceed to consider measures offered in the Senate from 1979 to the present, all but 52 were offered either by the majority leader or apparently at his direction. In the eight most recent Congresses (2007-2024), the number of motions to proceed offered per Congress has been significantly greater than before. Reasons for this increase may relate to changes in (1) the use of daily adjournments rather than recesses, (2) the way cloture is used in relation to these motions, or (3) the degree of deference paid to the majority leader in the exercise of his scheduling function. 
Few motions to proceed are defeated outright, because those unlikely to command majority support are seldom offered, and those that are not adopted usually reach no final vote (for example, because they are withdrawn). Of the 52 motions not offered by direction of the majority leader, by contrast, the Senate adopted 18, defeated 21, and laid 6 on the table. Five were abandoned after the Senate rejected cloture and two were ruled out of order.
Of these 52 motions, 37 were nondebatable because they addressed privileged matters (nearly all of them subject to expedited procedures under budgetary statutes or for congressional disapproval of executive action). Of the 52 motions, 42 occurred in the eight most recent Congresses (2009-2024), including 34 of the 42 that were nondebatable under expedited procedure statutes. These 42 motions also include 17 of the 23 offered by the minority leader and 20 of the 21 that the Senate defeated outright.
